entries.title: Shinji Ikari
entries.body: Gendo and Yui's son, summoned to Tokyo-3 by the father who abandoned him and put in the cockpit of Unit-01 the day he arrives. Withdrawn and conflict-averse, his search for a reason to exist beyond "the boy his father needs" is the show's emotional spine.

entries.scene: Wheeled in on a stretcher, too injured to pilot
entries.title: Rei Ayanami
entries.body: A quiet, compliant pilot grown rather than born — cloned from Yui Ikari's remains using the Angel Lilith's genetic material. Multiple physical copies of her exist in Terminal Dogma; the show is coy about how much continuity of self survives between them.

links.label: Where the clones live

An early episode built around her getting hurt
Her first extended inner monologue
Her fraught elevator scene with Asuka

entries.title: Misato Katsuragi
entries.body: Commands Eva deployment in the field and takes Shinji in as a housemate. A Second Impact survivor whose father died in the disaster that created it, which shapes both her drive to fight the Angels and her difficulty staying close to anyone.

links.label: The disaster that shaped her
The flashback that spells this out directly

entries.title: Gendo Ikari
entries.body: Runs NERV and, through it, humanity's entire Angel defense as cover for a private goal: using the Human Instrumentality Project to reunite with his dead wife Yui, whose soul he believes persists inside Unit-01. Treats nearly everyone, including Shinji, as an instrument toward that end.

links.label: What he's actually building toward
How sympathetic is that, really?
How he's shot, from the start
A rare, stark display of his temper
One of his only unguarded moments with Shinji

entries.title: Ritsuko Akagi
entries.body: Oversees the Evangelions and the MAGI supercomputers, inheriting both her position and a tangled personal history from her mother, Naoko Akagi, the MAGI's original designer.

links.label: The system she inherited
Her biggest test of that inheritance
Her complicated relationship with her mother

entries.title: Second Impact (September 13, 2000)
entries.body: A catastrophic explosion at an Antarctic research site, publicly blamed on a meteorite. It melted the polar ice caps, shifted the Earth's axis, and killed roughly half the world's population. Later revealed as the result of a deliberate contact experiment on the being called Adam. One knock-on effect stated directly in the Japanese Wikipedia entry: the axis tilt erased Japan's seasons entirely, leaving the country in permanent summer-like weather for the rest of the series.

links.label: What was actually experimented on
One survivor's firsthand account of it

quote.original: 西暦2000年9月13日に起きた大災害セカンドインパクト...セカンドインパクトの影響で地軸が捻じ曲がり、日本には四季がなくなり、1年中夏の状態になっている。
quote.translation: "The great disaster known as Second Impact, which occurred on September 13, 2000 AD... Due to Second Impact's effects, the Earth's axis was bent out of alignment; Japan lost its four seasons and has remained in a summer-like state year-round ever since."

entries.title: Tokyo-3 and the Angel War
entries.body: Fifteen years after Second Impact, the fortified city of Tokyo-3 is built over NERV's geofront headquarters specifically to fight the Angels, whose periodic attacks make up the bulk of the series' episodic structure. Mapped onto real-world geography, Tokyo-3 sits on the north shore of Lake Ashi, in Hakone, Kanagawa Prefecture — nowhere near the real Tokyo.

quote.original: 設定にある第3新東京市とは、実際の日本地図に当てはめると、神奈川県足柄下郡箱根町仙石原付近の芦ノ湖北岸あたりになる。
quote.translation: "Tokyo-3, as established in the setting, corresponds — when mapped onto an actual map of Japan — to around the north shore of Lake Ashi, near Sengokuhara, Hakone Town, Ashigarashimo District, Kanagawa Prefecture."

entries.title: NERV
entries.body: A UN-supervised paramilitary organization, publicly tasked with defending humanity from the Angels using the Evangelions. It answers, less publicly, to SEELE and to Gendo Ikari's own agenda.

links.label: Who NERV really answers to
A rival robot program NERV has to contend with
The shell-company front NERV pulls its pilots through

quote.original: 特務機関NERV（ネルフ） - 使徒殲滅を主要任務とする組織。EVAを保有。本部は第3新東京市の地下空間（ジオフロント）に位置する。
quote.translation: "The Special Task Agency NERV — an organization whose principal mission is Angel annihilation. It possesses the Evangelions. Its headquarters is located in the underground space (the Geofront) beneath Tokyo-3."

entries.title: Angels (Shito)
entries.body: The beings NERV exists to fight, each biologically and tactically distinct, sharing an AT Field and a strong drive to reach Lilith in Terminal Dogma. Their exact origin and nature is never pinned down on-screen.

links.label: What are they, really?
Where the Angels' individual names actually come from

entries.title: The Angels' names come from apocrypha and occult grimoires, not the Bible itself
entries.body: Most of the show's Angel names don't come from the canonical Bible at all, but from a long tradition of extra-biblical Jewish and Christian angelology — apocryphal texts like the Book of Enoch, mystical works like the Zohar, and later occult grimoires such as The Heptameron and The Nuctemeron — the same body of medieval and early-modern angel-and-demon classification that underlies much of the celestial-hierarchy pop culture still recycled in manga today. Most angel names in this tradition follow theophory, tacking a form of "-el" (god) onto a root word; Kaworu's Angel name, Tabris, notably breaks that pattern.

links.label: Back to the Angels generally
Sachiel's specific textual origin
Why Tabris is the exception to the naming pattern

entries.title: Sachiel: "the covering of God"
entries.body: Sachiel's name ("the covering of God") appears in Jewish occult texts as early as the 1200s and again in the 16th-century grimoire The Heptameron, and the Book of Enoch counts him among the Archangels alongside the better-known Michael, Uriel, and Raphael. Unlike the Angel he lends his name to, mythological Sachiel has no stories of interacting with humans directly — occult texts instead invoke him, like a minor deity, for help with legal and financial matters.

links.label: The wider naming pattern this fits
The Angel itself, being devoured by Unit-01

entries.title: AT Field
entries.body: "Absolute Terror Field": a barrier every Angel and Evangelion projects, physically blocking conventional weapons. Late in the series it's reframed less as a shield and more as the boundary that keeps one soul separate from every other.

links.label: The plan to dissolve it entirely
An entire operation built to pierce one

entries.title: Evangelions
entries.body: Giant bio-mechanical units, piloted via synchronization with a teenage pilot's nervous system, built as humanity's only weapon capable of matching an Angel's AT Field. Their organic, unwilling-looking behavior under stress is a recurring source of unease.

links.label: The first sign they might be alive

entries.title: What are the Angels, biologically or metaphysically?
entries.body: "Offspring of Adam" is as precise as the show gets. Whether they're organisms, weapons, something closer to concepts, or all three depending on continuity is never fixed — and the Rebuild films decline to answer it too.

links.label: The Adam/Lilith mapping is shaky too

entries.title: Humanity is officially the 18th Angel
entries.body: NERV's own numbered Angel list (as reproduced on Japanese Wikipedia) runs Adam (1st) and Lilith (2nd) as the two progenitor Angels, Sachiel through Tabris/Kaworu as the 3rd through 17th, and then lists Lilin — humanity itself — as the 18th Angel. The show never dwells on this classification, but it quietly puts humans and the things they're fighting in the same taxonomic category.

links.label: The 3rd–17th Angels NERV actually fights
The 17th Angel, whose classification is its own can of worms

quote.original: 第18使徒　リリン　人類全体を示す。
quote.translation: "18th Angel: Lilin — denotes humanity as a whole."

entries.title: Sailor Moon's fingerprints on the cast
entries.body: Several casting/naming choices trace back to Anno's fandom of Sailor Moon (which aired just before Eva): Misato's voice actress Kotono Mitsuishi was cast partly on the strength of her Usagi/Sailor Moon performance; Rei Ayanami's given name comes from Sailor Mars's civilian name, Hino Rei; and Kaworu Nagisa was modeled in part on Sailor Moon staffer Kunihiko Ikuhara, whom Anno was personally close with.

links.label: Misato
Rei
Kaworu

quote.original: その影響で、『セーラームーン』の主人公・月野うさぎ役の三石琴乃を葛城ミサトの声優に起用したり、綾波レイの名前が火野レイより採られたりしている。
quote.translation: "As a result of that influence, Kotono Mitsuishi — who played Sailor Moon protagonist Usagi Tsukino — was cast as the voice of Misato Katsuragi, and Rei Ayanami's name was taken from Hino Rei [Sailor Mars]."

entries.title: Anno wrote it, but didn't direct it
entries.body: Hideaki Anno — the series' overall director — wrote this episode's script himself, but the episode itself was directed by his assistant director, Kazuya Tsurumaki, with Anno and Masayuki assisting on storyboards. Series-director-as-episode-director isn't a given even on a show this personal to Anno.

links.label: The writing-credit breakdown for the whole series
The direction-credit breakdown for the whole series

entries.title: A year of planning, then six months just for this script
entries.body: Gainax began planning the series in July 1993 and held its first internal project meeting that September, but actual production on episodes 1–2 didn't start until September 1994 — a full year later. Anno has said the script for this episode alone took six months to finish; production wrapped in April 1995, six months before the October broadcast.

links.label: How that lead time ran out later

entries.title: Only 12 of 26 episodes were done when the show went on air
entries.body: By the time "Angel Attack" actually broadcast, Gainax had completed only twelve episodes after nearly two years of production — leaving the remaining fourteen to be finished in roughly a third of the time already spent. This compressed schedule is widely identified as the root of the severe production problems that hit the second half of the series.

links.label: Where that time crunch ends up
Who else was involved in getting the show made

entries.title: Where "I mustn't run away" actually comes from
entries.body: Shinji's refrain is traced by several sources to Anno's own life: he has described feeling "completely destroyed" after finishing Nadia: The Secret of Blue Water, spent four difficult years before Evangelion, and returned to anime work carrying the same resolve the line expresses. Gainax co-founder Yasuhiro Takeda has separately said the phrase traces further back, to the director's shelved project Blue Uru — and has suggested, more broadly, that Evangelion itself may just be a reflection of Anno's feelings during that period.

links.label: How the line changes by the finale
The broader reading of the finale as Anno's own story
The parable the show pairs this refrain with

quote.original: このセリフは、シリーズ公開前の4年間に困難な時期を過ごし、そこから同様の理念を持ってアニメ制作に復帰した庵野秀明自身の個人的な経験から着想を得たものである。
quote.translation: "This line was inspired by Hideaki Anno's own personal experience: he spent four difficult years before the series' release, and returned to anime production from that period carrying the same conviction."

entries.scene: Shinji sees a silent figure resembling Rei in the empty streets before Gendo summons him
entries.title: The Rei who shouldn't be there yet
entries.body: Early in this episode, alone in the deserted streets near Tokyo-3, Shinji glimpses what looks like Rei Ayanami — before he's ever met her. It isn't the "real" Rei on-screen at that point in the story, and multiple critics/scholars connect the apparition to The End of Evangelion's Instrumentality sequence, in which Rei-like figures appear to the dying as "messengers of redemption" guiding them into the merged whole. One reading (Nebbia) goes further: this is Rei appearing to Shinji backward across time, already on her way to godhood.

links.label: The later scene this apparition is read against
The soul-nature theory this feeds

quote.original: 本話の冒頭、シンジは第3新東京市近郊の無人の街で綾波レイの幻影を目撃する。このシーンに現れるレイは実在するレイではなく、その出現はテレビシリーズの完結編として1997年に公開された映画『新世紀エヴァンゲリオン劇場版 Air/まごころを、君に』の内容と関連付けられている。
quote.translation: "At the start of this episode, Shinji glimpses an apparition of Rei Ayanami in the deserted streets near Tokyo-3. The Rei who appears in this scene isn't the real Rei — her appearance here has been linked to the content of the 1997 film The End of Evangelion, released as the TV series' conclusion."

entries.scene: Shinji is shown Unit-01 in its hangar as Gendo appears above him
entries.title: Eva-01 staged as the mother in the room
entries.body: Scholars (Betty Stojnic, Claudio Cordella) read this episode's hangar scene as staging a full Freudian family triad on-screen: Shinji dwarfed between his distant, authoritative father above him and a maternal Eva-01 beside him — Eva-01 later raises its arm to shield Shinji, read as a maternal gesture rather than a mechanical reflex. It's the earliest visual argument for the idea that Yui's presence is somehow in the machine itself.

links.label: The theory this staging feeds

entries.title: Gendo is staged to be unreadable from episode 1 on
entries.body: From his very first scenes, Gendo is shot with his face partly hidden behind clasped hands, or behind glasses that reflect the monitor screens rather than showing his eyes. Scholar William Routt reads this as a deliberate graphic metaphor for a man who holds authority precisely by never revealing what he actually feels or intends — a visual rule the show keeps up for most of Gendo's screen time.

links.label: Back to Gendo himself

entries.scene: Misato's photo/note to Shinji
entries.title: An ongoing critical argument over Misato's introduction
entries.body: Misato's introductory note to Shinji includes a risqué photo of herself — read by some critics/scholars (Afanasov, Arbonés) as straightforward fan service sexualizing a female character for a young male audience, and by others as characterization consistent with Misato's personality. Writer Andrew M. Winters has linked the moment forward to the TV finale, where Misato tries to spur Shinji into the Eva by kissing him and promising sex afterward — read by some as the same device recurring at the story's most serious moment, and by others as something else entirely by then.

links.label: Back to Misato's introduction

entries.scene: The JSSDF's missile barrage against Sachiel
entries.title: A Macross homage, and a pile of tokusatsu references
entries.body: The opening missile-barrage attack on Sachiel visually quotes the "Itano Circus" — the swarming-missile animation technique from Macross, a series Anno and other future Gainax staff worked on as animators before Evangelion. Beyond that one homage, critic Philip Brophy describes the episode's opening minutes as a dense collage of Japanese tokusatsu/kaiju quotations (Godzilla, Ultra Q, Mazinger Z, Yamato, Gundam), and the episode borrows visual language from director Akio Jissoji's own distinctive style. Real-world military hardware appears throughout, including Type 74 tanks, Yak-38-inspired VTOLs, and M270 MLRS launchers.

entries.title: How episode 1 landed, then and later
entries.body: "Angel Attack" scored a 6.8% household rating on its original broadcast and later placed 17th in an Animage magazine "Animage Grand Prix" poll of favorite episode subtitles; the scene where Shinji and Rei first meet separately placed 16th in a TV Asahi viewer survey of the best anime scenes ever. At the 2006 Tokyo International Anime Fair, fans voted the first two episodes the anime installment they'd most like to watch again. Separately, novelist/scenario writer Kinoko Nasu (Fate/stay night, Tsukihime) has said watching this episode is what made him start writing.

entries.title: "Is that person really happy?" — Anno on his own audience
entries.body: In an interview during production of the first two episodes, Anno directly questioned the happiness of his own target audience — adult fans of robot anime and "bishōjo" anime — and said making the show was partly an attempt to work out what "happiness" could even mean for someone like that. It's about as blunt a statement of the show's self-critical relationship to its own audience as exists anywhere in its production history, well before the finale made that theme explicit.

links.label: Where this attitude resurfaces at the end

quote.original: たとえば、２０歳を過ぎてロボットアニメや美少女アニメが好きな人間って、本当に幸福なんでしょうか。（中略）この作品をつくりながら、そんな人間にとっての幸福ってなんなんだろうって考えてみたいんですよ。
quote.translation: "For instance, is a person over the age of twenty who likes robot anime and bishōjo anime really happy? [...] While making this work, I wanted to try thinking about what 'happiness' could even mean for a person like that."

entries.scene: Unit-01 runs out of power mid-battle but keeps fighting
entries.title: Unit-01's power runs out — and it keeps fighting anyway
entries.body: Cut off from its external power cable, Unit-01 should shut down; instead it goes into a silent, feral rampage, tearing Sachiel apart with its bare hands and biting into the Angel's core. It's the first on-screen sign of the Evangelions' unexplained not-quite-machine nature, well before the show says anything explicit about it.

links.label: The later, more explicit berserk episode
One reading of why it happens at all

entries.scene: Shinji wakes in a NERV hospital bed after the battle
entries.title: "Unfamiliar Ceiling"
entries.body: The episode's Japanese title, 見知らぬ、天井 ("Unfamiliar Ceiling"), names the shot of Shinji waking disoriented in a hospital bed after Unit-01's rampage — a framing device the series returns to more than once whenever Shinji wakes up somewhere that isn't home.

links.label: What put him there

entries.title: Shinji moves in with Misato
entries.body: Rather than send Shinji back to the guardian he'd been living with before NERV summoned him, Misato takes him into her own apartment at this episode's end — the arrangement that structures most of the series' domestic, non-battle scenes going forward.

links.label: Back to Misato's introduction

entries.title: Toji Suzuhara
entries.body: A blunt, athletic classmate of Shinji's whose younger sister was hurt as civilian collateral during Unit-01's battle with Sachiel — he confronts and punches Shinji over it before eventually becoming one of his closer friends. His arc later takes a much darker turn once he's drafted as a pilot.

links.label: The battle that hurt his sister
Where his story goes later

entries.title: Kensuke Aida
entries.body: A military-otaku classmate of Shinji's, more fascinated by the Evangelions and NERV's hardware than afraid of them; he and Toji round out the trio of friends around Shinji that gives the show most of its ordinary-teenager scenes amid the Angel attacks.

links.label: The friend he's usually paired with

entries.title: "The Phone That Doesn't Ring"
entries.body: The episode's Japanese title, 鳴らない、電話 ("The Phone That Doesn't Ring"), points at Shinji waiting for a call from Gendo that never comes, even as he starts to settle into an ordinary school routine with Misato, Toji, and Kensuke.

links.label: The father who doesn't call

entries.title: Shamshel's attack, and the crowd that comes to watch
entries.body: The Angel Shamshel attacks Tokyo-3 while Shinji is at school; Toji and Kensuke sneak out to watch Unit-01 fight from a hillside, one of the show's few scenes of ordinary civilians treating an Angel battle as a spectacle rather than a catastrophe.

links.label: One of the classmates watching
What NERV later recovers from Shamshel's remains
Where the name Shamshel comes from

entries.title: Shamshel: "sun of God", guardian of Eden
entries.body: Shamshel's name means "sun of God"; the Jewish mystical text the Zohar describes an angel by this name as the guardian posted at the Garden of Eden — matching Genesis 3:24's flaming-sword-wielding sentry. The Angel's design, a humanoid with two long, light-based whip arms that burn through whatever they strike, is a plausible visual echo of that flaming weapon, though animator Yoshitoh Asari's own account of the design's origin isn't on record.

links.label: The naming pattern this fits
The Angel this name belongs to

entries.title: The Hedgehog's Dilemma
entries.body: The episode takes its English title from Schopenhauer's parable (by way of Freud): hedgehogs huddling for warmth keep pricking each other with their spines, and must find a distance close enough to share warmth but far enough to avoid pain. It's presented as the closest thing the series has to an explicit thesis statement for Shinji's relationships — with Misato, with Toji and Kensuke, and eventually with everyone else in his life.

links.label: How Shinji tests that distance in this same episode
The refrain that runs alongside it
The one episode Anno didn't personally script

entries.scene: Shinji leaves Tokyo-3 alone after the battle
entries.title: Shinji's first attempt to just leave
entries.body: After the Shamshel battle, Shinji boards a train out of Tokyo-3 alone, seriously considering not coming back at all, before ultimately returning — the first full dry run of the running-away-and-returning pattern the show repeats for him right through the finale.

links.label: The idea the episode hangs this on
Where that pattern ends up by episode 26

entries.scene: Shinji delivers Rei's replacement student ID to her apartment
entries.title: Rei's apartment as a portrait of her lack of self
entries.body: Sent to deliver Rei's ID card after an Eva testing accident hospitalizes her, Shinji finds her apartment nearly bare — barely furnished, barely lived-in, with used bandages left out and almost nothing personal on display. Critics read the space itself as characterization: a person who has never been given, or allowed herself, much of an identity to decorate a room with.

links.label: Back to Rei's introduction
The larger question this scene feeds

entries.scene: Shinji picks up a photo and Gendo's spare glasses in Rei's apartment
entries.title: The slap over Gendo's glasses
entries.body: Among the few personal items in Rei's apartment, Shinji finds a photo of a young Gendo and Yui, plus a spare pair of Gendo's glasses — implying a relationship between Gendo and Rei closer than commander-and-pilot. When Gendo later catches Shinji holding the glasses, he slaps him and orders him to leave them alone, one of the starkest displays of Gendo's temper toward his son in the whole series.

links.label: Back to Gendo
The scene this happens right after

entries.title: Ramiel's drilling attack
entries.body: The Angel Ramiel — a stationary, geometrically simple Angel — begins drilling straight down toward NERV's Geofront headquarters, forcing a defense built around holding a fixed position rather than the mobile fights of earlier episodes. Rei is hurt again defending the position, continuing this stretch of the show's focus on her as a character rather than just a second pilot.

links.label: Back to Rei
The plan built to finish Ramiel off
Where the name Ramiel comes from

entries.title: Ramiel: a fallen angel from the Book of Enoch
entries.body: The Book of Enoch — an apocryphal text attributed to Noah's great-grandfather, fleshing out the fallen-angel and Nephilim mythology behind Genesis's flood — names Ramiel as one of the leaders of the angels corrupted through contact with humanity. A separate text, the Apocalypse of Baruch, credits him with ruling over "true visions." Whether either association shaped the Angel's crystalline, self-reflective design in the show, or whether Anno was simply nodding to the tokusatsu series Future Police Urashiman as he's said elsewhere, is untested either way.

links.label: The naming pattern this fits
The Angel this name belongs to

entries.title: Operation Yashima
entries.body: To pierce Ramiel's AT Field, NERV draws power from the entire Japanese electrical grid to fire a single positron-rifle shot — a citywide blackout mobilized around one attack, and one of the series' clearest illustrations of just how much of Japan's remaining infrastructure exists to keep the Angel fight going.

links.label: The Angel this is built to kill
The barrier the whole operation exists to pierce

entries.title: Jet Alone
entries.body: A rival, conventionally-powered giant robot, Jet Alone, is unveiled by a Japanese government agency as a possible non-Eva alternative to NERV's defense program — and immediately malfunctions during its public demonstration, running rampant with an armed nuclear reactor on board. Unlike most of the series' crises, this one has nothing to do with the Angels at all; it's framed as pure institutional rivalry.

links.label: The organization Jet Alone was built to compete with

entries.title: One of the series' lighter episodes
entries.body: With no Angel involved, this episode leans into physical comedy and workplace farce — Misato and Ritsuko racing to shut Jet Alone down manually — a deliberate tonal break between the darker material building up around Rei and Gendo in the episodes just before and after it.

links.label: The incident this episode is built around

entries.scene: The aircraft carrier convoy brings Unit-02 and Asuka to Japan
entries.title: Asuka and Unit-02 arrive in Japan
entries.body: Asuka Langley Souryuu makes her first on-screen appearance being transported to Japan by an aircraft-carrier convoy alongside the newly built, already field-tested Evangelion Unit-02 — introduced immediately as brash, multilingual, and openly contemptuous of Shinji's comparative inexperience as a pilot.

links.label: Her fuller introduction
The NERV agent escorting her

entries.title: Unit-02: already combat-tested before Japan ever sees it
entries.body: Unlike Units 00 and 01, Unit-02 arrives in Japan with prior field experience under Asuka's piloting — part of what the show uses to establish the pecking order between her and Shinji before they ever fight side by side.

links.label: The arrival this establishes

entries.title: Gaghiel attacks the carrier convoy
entries.body: The aquatic Angel Gaghiel ambushes the same aircraft-carrier convoy transporting Unit-02, forcing Shinji and Asuka into their first fight together. Gaghiel drags Unit-02 underwater mid-battle; Misato's crews finish it off by lodging two sunken battleships in its jaws and opening fire with everything left in the convoy — no synchronized piloting required yet, unlike the very next Angel they face.

links.label: The convoy this attacks
The next Angel, which does demand real coordination

entries.title: Israfel splits into two identical copies
entries.body: The Angel Israfel attacks Tokyo-3 and, after apparently being defeated, splits into two fully identical copies that each overpower a separate Eva. Beating it requires Shinji and Asuka to fight as a single coordinated unit rather than two pilots improvising separately — the problem Misato's subsequent training regimen is built to solve.

links.label: The previous battle, fought with no coordination needed
The training this attack makes necessary
Where the name Israfel comes from

entries.title: Israfel: the angel of music and the last trumpet
entries.body: Israfel is traditionally the angel of music — Edgar Allan Poe's poem "Israfel" describes him singing with a "lyre" of unusually expressive strings — and, per the 14th-century Arabic text The Wonders of Creation, the angel who will sound the trumpet marking the end of all earthly life, weeping at the sight of Hell while he waits for God's order to do it. He's also said to have tutored Muhammad. In the show, the Angel Israfel's defining trait is splitting into two identical bodies that can only be beaten by a synchronized, music-timed dual attack — a fight the episode literally choreographs to a beat.

links.label: The naming pattern this fits
The Angel this name belongs to
The music-timed fight this mythology maps onto directly

entries.title: Forced synchronization, and the dance metaphor
entries.body: Misato has Shinji and Asuka train together like dance partners so their combined movements read as a single, coordinated fighter rather than two separate pilots working against each other — the source of the episode's title, and an early example of the show using a mundane, non-military metaphor (dancing) to frame what piloting an Eva actually demands of two people.

links.label: The fight this training is for
Back to Asuka

entries.title: Episodes 10 and 11 were swapped during production
entries.body: Gainax's 1993 planning document originally slated the magma-dive Angel-capture story as episode 11 and a NERV-blackout story as episode 10; during production the two were swapped, so the magma story became episode 10 ("Magmadiver") and the blackout draft became episode 11 ("The Day Tokyo-3 Stood Still") instead.

links.label: The blackout episode this became

entries.title: Sandalphon's design comes from a documentary about ancient life
entries.body: The dormant, larval Angel Sandalphon — found in a volcano's magma chamber — was designed with inspiration from an NHK documentary, Life: A Long Journey of 4 Billion Years, specifically its depiction of the prehistoric predator Anomalocaris; trilobites are cited as a secondary influence. Writer Virginie Nebbia has separately argued the episode's battle staging draws on David Brin's novel Sundiver.

links.label: The broader question of what Angels even are
Where the name Sandalphon comes from

entries.title: Sandalphon: the prophet Elijah, reborn as an angel who watches over children
entries.body: In Jewish tradition, Sandalphon is the biblical prophet Elijah, transformed into angelic form after ascending to Heaven; Elijah is associated with unborn and newborn children, and a seat is traditionally reserved for him at circumcision ceremonies. As Sandalphon he's said to be able to reach any part of the earth — a trait the show echoes by having its own Sandalphon dwell inside a volcano. The mythological tie to children lines up with the Angel's design: a small, larval creature that cries like a human infant before metamorphosing into a prehistoric-fish shape.

links.label: The naming pattern this fits
The documentary that shaped its actual on-screen design

entries.title: "Magmadiver", by way of a novel Anno never read
entries.body: Anno has confirmed in interview that the episode's English title was inspired by David Brin's 1980 novel Sundiver — while also stating flatly that he never actually read it, just picked up the title.

entries.scene: Misato's naked body, seen in the episode's final scene
entries.title: A scar that pays off two episodes later
entries.body: The final scene of "Magmadiver" shows Misato's bare torso, including a scar later revisited directly in episode 12's flashback to her Second Impact trauma. Evangelion Chronicle argues the scene is doing more than fan service — it's quietly seeding Misato's connection to the disaster two episodes ahead of the reveal.

links.label: The flashback this sets up
The disaster itself

entries.title: Asuka pilots out of rivalry with Rei, not duty
entries.body: According to Evangelion Chronicle, Asuka's decision to take on the Sandalphon mission alone is driven less by a sense of duty to NERV than by simple competitiveness with Rei — an early, explicit statement of the rivalry that structures most of Asuka's choices as a pilot going forward.

links.label: Back to Asuka
The rival she measures herself against

entries.title: Highest rating yet, most divisive reviews yet
entries.body: "Magmadiver" drew a 9.5% household rating — the highest for the series to that point — but landed an ambivalent-to-negative critical reception, frequently singled out as the closest the show gets to pure filler and criticized for leaning hard on fan service (Asuka's swimsuit scene, Misato's ending shot). Other reviewers pushed back, defending its humor, the tension of the magma-chamber battle, and Shinji's rescue of Asuka as one of his better moments.

links.label: The same critical argument, first raised back in episode 1

entries.title: A sabotage blackout, and the first three-Eva team-up
entries.body: NERV headquarters loses power to unidentified sabotage just as the Angel Matarael arrives; with electricity out, Gendo and staff activate the Evangelions manually, and Shinji, Rei, and Asuka fight together for the first time as a genuine three-pilot team, with Shinji landing the finishing shot.

links.label: The production swap that put this story here
Their first two-pilot coordination, two episodes earlier

entries.title: A title borrowed from a 1951 sci-fi classic
entries.body: The English title directly echoes the 1951 film The Day the Earth Stood Still, one of several NGE episode titles that reference existing science fiction cinema; the episode's storyboard-stage English title was the more mundane "Panic in Geo Front" before the change. Anno's fondness for genre callbacks shows up again here in a UCC coffee can visible on-screen, the same brand featured in his earlier series Gunbuster.

entries.scene: Gendo personally helps NERV staff manually activate the Evangelions
entries.title: Gendo's one unusually warm moment
entries.body: Normally cold and unapproachable, Gendo pitches in directly to help his subordinates get the Evas running without power — a rare glimpse of him as responsible and human rather than purely instrumental, and one that visibly surprises Shinji. Writer Dennis Redmond calls it unusual by the norms of Japanese storytelling, which "tends to recognise group achievement rather than individual merit."

links.label: How he's usually shot instead
How quickly that warmth can flip, one episode earlier

entries.scene: Asuka mocks Rei's calm under pressure by calling her "Miss Perfect"
entries.title: "Miss Perfect", and the masculine-protest reading of Asuka
entries.body: Asuka's hostility toward Rei's composure under fire — she calls her yūtōsei, "honor student" or "Miss Perfect" — has been read by critics (including editor Gualtiero Cannarsi) through the lens of "masculine protest", a psychological term for rebellion by women weary of a stereotyped gender role: Asuka tries to out-perform and out-tough everyone around her, fusing an inferiority complex with radical rivalry. The episode ends with her softening toward Rei as a teammate for the first time.

links.label: The same rivalry, one episode earlier
Where this pattern finally breaks her down

entries.scene: The three pilots lie on a hillside after the battle, watching Tokyo-3's lights come back on
entries.title: Why does humanity even fight the Angels?
entries.body: Shinji wonders aloud, after the battle, what the Angels' attacks are actually for — a question the show raises here and never really answers. Writer Rob Vuckovich reads it as evidence that God is functionally absent or indifferent in Evangelion's world, despite NERV's own motto ("God's in His Heaven, All's right with the World").

links.label: The deeper unknown this question sits on top of

entries.title: One of the best-reviewed episodes of the run
entries.body: "The Day Tokyo-3 Stood Still" drew a 9.0% household rating and was widely praised — critics singled out Matarael's battle, the episode's pacing and script, its positive tone, and its handling of philosophical questions about technology and human agency.

entries.title: A scrapped Angel called Turel, and the actual Sahaquiel fight
entries.body: The episode's original planning-document draft cast a different Angel, Turel ("the rock of God"), as the antagonist; it was replaced during production by Sahaquiel, a satellite-sized Angel that tries to crash-land onto NERV using its own body as a bomb. All three Evas team up to destroy it against NERV's own odds, with Asuka landing the final blow.

links.label: The previous episode's three-pilot fight

entries.scene: A sepia-toned flashback to Misato at fourteen, at the South Pole
entries.title: Misato's Second Impact flashback
entries.body: The episode opens with a flashback revealing that fourteen-year-old Misato was present at the South Pole when Second Impact occurred, and that her father died there; she alone survived. It's the clearest on-screen account yet of how the disaster made her who she is, and it directly follows up the scar glimpsed at the end of the previous episode.

links.label: Back to Misato's introduction
The disaster itself
The scar that foreshadowed this, one episode earlier

entries.scene: Gendo compliments Shinji after the Sahaquiel battle
entries.title: Shinji realizes he pilots for his father's approval
entries.body: After Gendo unexpectedly praises him, Shinji recognizes that the real reason he keeps getting in the Eva is to earn that approval — not duty, not saving the world. Newtype magazine calls Gendo's praise a "double-edged sword": it gives Shinji a reason to keep piloting, but ties his self-worth to a father who is otherwise withholding, a dynamic the series revisits explicitly in episode 16.

links.label: How coldly Gendo treated him from episode 1
Another rare warm moment, one episode earlier

entries.scene: A maritime convoy transports a giant sealed object toward Antarctica
entries.title: First glimpse of the Spear of Longinus
entries.body: This episode gives the first on-screen look at the Spear of Longinus, a massive artifact being shipped by sea — named for the legendary Roman soldier whose spear pierced the crucified Christ, and for the belief that whoever wields it, blood-soaked, commands the world. Its full significance and destination aren't spelled out yet.

entries.title: Adam as a giant of light, and Sodom and Gomorrah in Antarctica
entries.body: The episode's opening flashback depicts Adam, the first Angel, as a colossal being of light — a form scholars have linked to Kabbalistic depictions of Adam "before his Fall" and to the giant of light from Ultraman 80. Later, Gendo and Fuyutsuki discuss Second Impact over shots of salt columns rising from Antarctica's reddened seas, an explicit visual reference to Lot's wife and the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah; Fuyutsuki calls the disaster a "punishment" and the pole itself a "real Dead Sea."

links.label: Adam's fuller introduction, later in the series
The disaster being discussed

entries.title: A generally well-liked episode — and an unlikely nod from Jordan Peele
entries.body: "She said, 'Don't make others suffer for your personal hatred'" drew a 7.4% rating and placed 12th in a 1996 Animage magazine readers' poll of best episodes. Reception was largely positive, with some critics calling out the plot as stock and the Sahaquiel fight as too brief. Decades later, Jordan Peele's production notes for the film Nope confirmed the design of its flying creature, Jean Jacket, was directly inspired by Evangelion's Angels — Peele specifically cited their "hyper minimalism" and "biomechanical design flair," and commentators drew a direct visual line to Sahaquiel's design.

entries.title: A battle fought entirely inside the Magi
entries.body: A microscopic Angel, Iruel, infiltrates NERV through a research chamber and rapidly evolves into something that behaves like a computer virus, attempting to hijack the Magi supercomputer into triggering NERV's self-destruct. Ritsuko Akagi defeats it not by force but with a "reverse hack": rather than fighting Iruel's evolution, she engineers a program that gets it to choose coexistence with the Magi instead.

links.label: The system under attack
Back to Ritsuko's introduction

entries.title: The abandoned three-episode "fear" arc, and where the schedule finally breaks
entries.body: This episode was originally drafted as "What Comes After Fear," the opening chapter of a planned three-episode arc in which Shinji would be defeated and trapped inside an Angel. Gainax abandoned the arc mid-production; some of its ideas were later folded into episode 16 instead. Wikipedia's account also marks this episode as the point where the show's chronic scheduling crisis becomes acute: only twelve episodes were finished when the series began airing, leaving the remaining fourteen to be made in about a third of the time already spent.

links.label: The same production crunch, described from episode 1's side

entries.title: The three Magi as a split portrait of one woman
entries.body: Casper, Melchior, and Balthasar are each modeled on a different facet of designer Naoko Akagi's personality — as scientist, mother, and woman, per the series' own film books. Writer Dennis Redmond reads the arrangement as a "clever gender bend" of the Christian Trinity; that Casper (associated with Naoko-as-woman) is the last of the three to resist Iruel's attack has been read as Ritsuko coming to understand her mother on that specific, human level.

links.label: The system itself

entries.scene: Ritsuko and Misato talk about Naoko during the Iruel operation
entries.title: Ritsuko, Naoko, and Evangelion's "cannibalistic" mothers
entries.body: Ritsuko admits during the operation that she never liked her mother, Naoko, whose personality is nonetheless imprinted permanently into the Magi she now depends on. Scholar Mariana Ortega notes Ritsuko physically entering the Magi's cabling mirrors how Eva pilots enter cockpits built around their own mothers' souls, and describes the mother figure across the series as metaphorically and literally "cannibalistic."

links.label: Back to Ritsuko
The parallel mother-in-the-machine theory for Shinji and Yui

entries.title: One animator's crash course in molecular biology, drafted into the script
entries.body: Animator Mitsuo Iso, largely self-taught in computer science and biology, wrote an early, much-denser draft of this episode's script full of real genetics terminology — polysomes, the Pribnow box, the central dogma of molecular biology, the sigma factor — deliberately modeled on structures like tRNA, and drew Central Dogma's own layout from The Andromeda Strain. Much of Iso's original draft was cut or reworked by Akio Satsukawa and Anno, but the terminology survived into the aired episode.

entries.title: A low rating, a strong critical response
entries.body: "Lilliputian Hitcher" drew only a 3.4% household rating but was well-reviewed, with critics praising its sense of suspense, the visual design of NERV's control rooms, its focus on Ritsuko, and the Iruel hacking sequence — Comic Book Resources ranked the fight as the second-best in the entire series.

entries.scene: Rei's extended stream-of-consciousness sequence during the pilot compatibility test
entries.title: Where Rei's monologue actually came from
entries.body: Anno has said he felt he'd been neglecting Rei as a character partway through the series, and set out to correct it here by writing her first extended inner monologue — originally conceived with Rei as a girl with schizophrenia. He struggled to write it convincingly until a friend lent him a book on mental illness containing a poem written by a person living with one; that poem gave him the words, and the monologue was written in a single sitting. It marks the point the series turns more explicitly introspective for its remaining episodes.

links.label: Back to Rei's introduction
The identity question this monologue circles without answering

entries.scene: Rei pilots Unit-00 to deliver the Spear of Longinus to Terminal Dogma
entries.title: The Spear reaches Terminal Dogma
entries.body: The Spear of Longinus, first glimpsed being shipped from Antarctica two episodes earlier, is delivered by Rei via Unit-00 to the deepest level of NERV's base — Terminal Dogma, the same restricted area that later turns out to hold Lilith.

links.label: The Spear's first appearance
What else is kept in Terminal Dogma

entries.scene: Shinji, briefly piloting Unit-00, glimpses a distorted image of Rei and it goes berserk
entries.title: Whose soul is really in Unit-00?
entries.body: When Shinji attempts to sync with Unit-00 instead of his usual Unit-01, it violently attacks the observation booth — and he glimpses a warped image of Rei in the process. Fans and critics have read this as evidence Unit-00 carries the soul of an earlier Rei clone (or, in one reading, of Naoko Akagi, given Ritsuko is present and resembles her mother in the same scene); the episode itself never says which, if either, is correct.

links.label: The equivalent unexplained incident for Unit-01
The later theory this feeds into

entries.scene: Kaji's investigation into Eva pilot selection
entries.title: The Marduk Institute
entries.body: Kaji's investigation surfaces the Marduk Institute, the body apparently responsible for selecting Evangelion pilot candidates — revealed to be a front for 108 shell companies rather than a real organization. One of those shells lists Gendo, Fuyutsuki, and SEELE's Keel Lorenz among its registered names, tying NERV's pilot-selection process directly back to the same people steering Instrumentality from behind it.

links.label: The organization these names ultimately answer to
The agency Marduk feeds pilots into

entries.scene: Shinji visits Yui's grave with Gendo for the first time in years
entries.title: An empty grave, and "humans survive by forgetting"
entries.body: Gendo takes Shinji to Yui's grave and admits there's no body under the stone — it's purely a place to remember her by — before adding that humans survive by forgetting. Scholars read the scene as one of the only moments Shinji and Gendo approach genuine mutual understanding, letting Shinji settle (however partially) why he was the one entrusted with fighting the Angels.

links.label: Back to Gendo
Where Yui actually persists, per one theory
Another of Gendo's rare unguarded moments

entries.scene: Asuka kisses Shinji out of boredom, then insists it meant nothing
entries.title: The first Shinji/Asuka kiss, and how much it actually means
entries.body: Bored and restless, Asuka kisses Shinji and immediately downplays it as nothing more than boredom — a lie critics (Fabio Bartoli among them) read as reassurance aimed at herself as much as at him. Commentators disagree sharply on how to take it: some read it as one of Asuka's worse impulsive moments toward Shinji, others as evidence both of them have real feelings for each other that neither is equipped to admit or act on.

links.label: Back to Asuka
The parable this dynamic keeps testing

entries.scene: A drunk, tearful Misato tells Kaji the real reason she left him
entries.title: Why Misato really left Kaji
entries.body: Misato admits to Kaji that she broke up with him years earlier because he reminded her too much of her father, with whom she had an unresolved, conflicted relationship. Some critics read this through Jung's Electra complex; more broadly, several commentators note Misato unconsciously searches every relationship for a father figure, then panics and withdraws once she finds the resemblance — the same pattern this scene names directly.

links.label: Back to Misato
The trauma underneath that pattern
Back to Kaji

entries.scene: Kaji shows Misato a crucified giant in Terminal Dogma, calling it Adam
entries.title: The giant Kaji calls "Adam" — except it isn't
entries.body: Kaji secretly brings Misato into Terminal Dogma and shows her a crucified, seven-eyed giant, identifying it as Adam, the first Angel. The series finale later reveals this figure is actually Lilith, the second Angel — one of several points across the show where characters' own labels for Adam and Lilith turn out to be unreliable.

links.label: Who this figure actually is
The wider pattern of Adam/Lilith mix-ups

entries.scene: The seven-eyed mask on the crucified giant, echoing SEELE's own emblem
entries.title: Seven eyes, and the Book of Revelation
entries.body: The seven-eyed mask on the giant in Terminal Dogma echoes SEELE's own emblem, and multiple scholars trace both to the Book of Revelation's lamb with "seven horns and seven eyes," described there as "the Seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth." Assistant director Kazuya Tsurumaki has said the show's Christian imagery was chosen largely for aesthetic and exoticizing effect on its Japanese audience, rather than to encode a specific theology.

links.label: The organization whose emblem this echoes

entries.title: A quiet, character-focused episode with a divisive kiss
entries.body: Without a single Angel battle, "Those women longed for the touch of others' lips, and thus invited their kisses" drew a 6% rating and split critics: some found the Misato/Kaji romance overwrought and Asuka's behavior toward Shinji indefensible, while others praised the same scenes' focus on character interiority, plus the episode's religious imagery and its use of Bach's Cello Suite No. 1 over Shinji's private cello practice.

entries.scene: Unit-01 is absorbed into Leliel's shadow
entries.title: Leliel, and the Dirac sea
entries.body: Leliel, the twelfth Angel, appears as a floating sphere over Tokyo-3; Ritsuko determines its true body is actually the shadow it casts on the ground, while the visible sphere is merely its shadow. Shinji, attacking alone out of wounded pride, is pulled into that shadow — a pocket dimension the show calls the Dirac sea, named after physicist Paul Dirac's theoretical sea of negative-energy particles, though the episode's usage is closer to "another dimension entirely" than the real physics concept.

links.label: The broader unknown this Angel adds to

entries.title: Two titles, two different references
entries.body: The English title refers to psychoanalyst Melanie Klein's concept of "splitting" — an infant's habit of dividing its perception of the mother's breast into a wholly "good" and wholly "bad" object rather than one complex whole. The Japanese title instead references Søren Kierkegaard's The Sickness Unto Death, on despair as the human condition; editor Yūichirō Oguro reads the title as pointing at Shinji's confrontation with himself inside Leliel. Anno has since admitted, bluntly, that he never actually read Kierkegaard's book past the first few pages and cited it mostly "out of pedantry, to seem intelligent."

links.label: The confrontation this title is read against
Another Anno title borrowed from a book he never finished

entries.scene: Suspended in the Dirac sea, Shinji argues with a younger version of himself on a train
entries.title: Shinji versus Shinji
entries.body: Trapped in a timeless void, Shinji has an extended dialogue with another version of himself, who coldly picks apart his weaknesses and tells him that other "Shinjis" exist inside everyone else's minds too — "they are all Ikari Shinji." The series' own film books describe the two Shinjis as literalizing Freud's ego and superego; other critics have compared the scene to psychoanalytic therapy, to Pirandello's theory that the self fragments into social masks, and to Sartre's "hell is other people."

links.label: Rei's own identity-questioning monologue, two episodes earlier
The same kind of identity question, asked of Rei instead

entries.scene: Unit-01 tears itself free of Leliel's shadow, screaming and covered in blood
entries.title: Eva-01's second birth, and the "bad breast"
entries.body: Unit-01 violently escapes Leliel under its own power, screaming and drenched in blood — critics uniformly read the image as a second, more literal birth. Yūichirō Oguro extends the episode's Kleinian framing directly onto the Evas themselves: Eva-01, trapping and nearly killing Shinji, reads as the "bad breast," while Yui's presence saving him at the last moment reads as the "good breast" — the same object split in two, exactly as Klein's theory describes.

links.label: Yui's presence this theory leans on
The Kleinian concept the title names

entries.scene: Inside the void, Shinji sees an image of Gendo praising him
entries.title: Even trapped and half-dead, Shinji still wants his father's approval
entries.body: Among the visions Shinji has while suspended in Leliel is his estranged father praising him — read as a source of spiritual strength Shinji clings to even here, and as evidence he still fundamentally fears Gendo while wanting his approval more than almost anything else. It's the same dynamic the series named explicitly four episodes earlier.

links.label: Where this dynamic was first spelled out, in episode 12

entries.scene: Asuka goads Shinji into fighting Leliel alone, calling it "a man's job"
entries.title: A masculine posture that collapses into a womb
entries.body: Provoked by Asuka, Shinji puts on an unusually confident, masculine front before attacking Leliel alone — then spends the rest of the episode passively curled in a fetal position inside a womb-like void, dependent on the women around him (Misato, Ritsuko, and ultimately Yui) to bring him back. Scholar Cristopher Smith reads the sequence as the show visibly undercutting the value of conventional masculinity in real time, right as Shinji tries hardest to perform it.

links.label: Back to Asuka
The birth imagery this passivity feeds into

entries.title: Where the abandoned "fear trilogy" actually landed
entries.body: This episode absorbs the leftover ideas from the three-episode arc Gainax scrapped back at episode 13 — its third chapter would have had Shinji absorbed by an Angel and attempting first contact with it, which becomes, in the aired version, Shinji absorbed into Leliel and left alone with only himself to talk to instead. Some of the same abandoned material was also folded into episode 19.

links.label: The original three-episode plan this replaced

entries.title: A turning point, and one of the show's best-reviewed episodes
entries.body: "Splitting of the Breast" drew a 9.4% rating, placed 16th in a 1996 Animage readers' poll, and is widely marked by critics as the point Evangelion shifts from a fairly conventional mecha series into what one critic called "an enigmatic character study" — the last episode, by most readings, before the show's back half fully commits to psychological introspection over monster-of-the-week plotting.

entries.title: Toji is confirmed as the Fourth Child, and Marduk is exposed as a front
entries.body: Eva-03 is airlifted from America to Japan with an unnamed new pilot; the episode never states outright that it's Toji, though the editing and staging make it obvious. Separately, Kaji confirms to Misato what episode 15 first implied: the Marduk Institute, supposedly responsible for selecting Eva pilots, doesn't actually exist — it's a shell built from over a hundred fictitious companies with Gendo hiding behind it.

links.label: Back to Toji
Where Marduk was first exposed

entries.title: A scrapped, more explicitly incestuous Gendo/Rei concept
entries.body: Assistant director Kazuya Tsurumaki has said staff originally conceived Rei as simultaneously a clone of Gendo's dead wife and, functionally, both a wife and daughter figure to him — a draft scene even had Rei waiting for Gendo naked in a tube. The concept was walked back for the aired series, and Tsurumaki has said the most compelling part of the finished dynamic is precisely that Gendo and Rei never act on the incestuous undertone the early concept implied.

links.label: Back to Rei
The scene that hints at some closeness between them

entries.scene: Misato is interrogated about Leliel's apparent attempt to communicate with Shinji
entries.title: The Instrumentality Committee, and Angels that might be learning
entries.body: A body called the Instrumentality Committee questions Misato over whether the Angel Leliel deliberately targeted Shinji psychologically. Afterward, Gendo tells Fuyutsuki plainly that the Angels are beginning to develop intelligence — the first explicit statement that NERV's enemies might be capable of learning and adapting, not just repeating the same kind of attack.

links.label: The project this committee is presumably tied to
The larger unknown about what the Angels are

entries.title: The S² engine gets a name
entries.body: Ritsuko names the "Super-Solenoid" engine here for the first time — an internal power source, acquired from the Angel Shamshel, that becomes central to the back half of the series once an Evangelion manages to absorb one for itself.

links.label: The Angel this engine was taken from
How NERV actually got hold of one

entries.title: The S² engine was salvaged from Shamshel's core
entries.body: Background dialogue added for the Renewal re-release makes explicit what the original broadcast only implies: while NERV staff dismantle Shamshel's remains, a technician announces a "power analysis unit" inbound from NERV's German 2nd Branch and orders a team to "place extreme priority on recovering the existing core." Gendo and Fuyutsuki turn up in person to inspect what's recovered, and, once satisfied, Gendo orders everything else discarded — Eva-04's ill-fated S² sample, later sent to America and installed with disastrous results, traces back to this scene.

links.label: The Angel this sample was taken from
What this implies about where the S² organ actually sits

entries.title: Is the S² organ physically inside the Eva's core?
entries.body: A long-running EvaGeeks forum thread (kicked off by poster ObsessiveMathsFreak) argues from two angles that an Eva or Angel's S² organ lives inside its core rather than being some separate structure: NERV's evident fixation on recovering Shamshel's core specifically when after an S² sample, and the way Unit-01 targets Zeruel's core precisely when it bites down and absorbs its S² engine. Posters ultimately converge on treating the core as a container — for a soul, and, where present, for an S² organ — rather than the core and the S² organ being identical. Frame-by-frame analysis posted to the thread backs this up: Eva-01's jaws in that scene close over Zeruel's nuclear region, not its face, despite the face being the last part visibly consumed.

links.label: The salvage operation that started the debate
The feeding scene used as visual evidence
The follow-on question of why Evas don't just have one already

entries.title: Why don't Units 00–02 grow their own S² organs?
entries.body: If Evangelions are derived from Adam just like the Angels, why doesn't NERV simply have one that comes with a working S² organ built in? Forum theories split two ways. One camp argues NERV engineered the trait out deliberately, at the genetic level — handing pilots of unknown reliability an effectively unlimited, un-killswitchable power source was too dangerous, so the umbilical cable stays as a built-in leash. A competing theory (from poster ObsessiveMathsFreak) ties it to the soul instead: since NERV can't manufacture a soul from nothing, and the core may only mature enough to support an S² organ once a soul is present to drive that growth, a soul-less Eva would never develop a functioning S² regardless of its genetics — leaving Angel salvage as the only way NERV ever gets one installed.

links.label: The premise this theory builds on
A later wrinkle in this same debate

entries.scene: Eva-03's activation test goes wrong mid-transport
entries.title: Bardiel possesses Eva-03 — with Toji still inside
entries.body: The Angel Bardiel possesses Eva-03 during its activation test, easily defeating both Rei's and Asuka's units. Shinji refuses to fight the possessed Eva-03, unwilling to risk killing whoever is piloting it — at which point Gendo overrides him entirely, using the Dummy System to force Unit-01 to destroy Eva-03 without Shinji's consent, only for Shinji (and the audience) to learn afterward that his friend Toji was in the cockpit the whole time.

links.label: Gendo's override, and what it costs Toji
Toji's selection as the pilot, one episode earlier

entries.title: Toji's amputation, and Anno's own father
entries.body: Anno reportedly considered killing Toji outright after the Bardiel incident, but had promised a producer early in production that he wouldn't kill child characters, so the staff settled on maiming him instead — Toji loses his left leg. Anno has connected the choice to his own father, who lost a leg in an accident and wore a prosthesis for the rest of his life; Anno has said the experience left him with a lasting fascination with deformity, tracing it back to a childhood robot show in which a mecha loses an arm, and that he came to believe he "could love only something that is stumpy."

links.label: Back to Toji

entries.title: Gendo vs. Shinji as the plank of Carneades
entries.body: Editor Yūichirō Oguro compares the Gendo/Shinji standoff over Eva-03 to the ancient dilemma of Carneades' plank — two shipwrecked men fighting over a single piece of wood that can only keep one of them alive, in which killing the other might be ethically defensible given the stakes. Gendo acts on that calculus without hesitation; Shinji's entire refusal is a rejection of it.

links.label: How sympathetic Gendo's ends-justify-means logic really is
The instrumental way Gendo has treated Shinji from the start

entries.title: The last episode made with (nearly) the full toolkit
entries.body: Around this episode and the next, Anno and Gainax staff privately concluded they could no longer finish the series to the standard they wanted within the remaining broadcast schedule — though they kept trying anyway, all the way to the end. "Ambivalence" and "Introjection" mark the last point the studio could still draw on virtually all its remaining production resources before the system properly broke down; Anno has said it was also around here that he finally settled on how the series would end.

links.label: How far back this production crunch actually started
Where this schedule collapse ultimately leads

entries.scene: Unit-01 runs out of power against Zeruel, then reactivates and eats it
entries.title: Zeruel, and Eva-01's second berserk feast
entries.body: The Angel Zeruel overwhelms Asuka's and Rei's Evas and nearly kills a depowered Unit-01 before Shinji's despair triggers a full, uncontrolled reactivation: Eva-01 devours Zeruel outright, absorbing its S² engine in the process and effectively gaining unlimited operating power. It's the same unpowered-berserk phenomenon from episode 2, taken to its most extreme form yet.

links.label: The earlier, smaller-scale version of this same phenomenon
The engine Eva-01 absorbs here
Fan analysis of exactly where this bite lands

entries.scene: Kaji talks to Shinji after Shinji quits NERV in protest over Toji
entries.title: Shinji chooses to fight for himself, not for his father
entries.body: After walking away from NERV over what happened to Toji, Shinji is talked back by Kaji, not Gendo — and critically, he returns to pilot Unit-01 having decided to do it for his own reasons rather than to win his father's approval, a break from the pattern the series named explicitly back in episode 12. Several scholars mark this as the point Shinji first claims something like a self-authored identity, even though the show immediately complicates it by having him waver again afterward.

links.label: The approval-seeking pattern this breaks from
Back to Kaji

entries.title: "Introjection": Shinji absorbing his father's rule about necessary sacrifice
entries.body: The episode's English title names the psychoanalytic process of taking another person's values in as your own. One reading, drawn from the series' own glossary material, is that by episode's end Shinji has introjected Gendo's underlying rule — that sacrifice is sometimes necessary in war — the same norm that later lets him bring himself to kill Kaworu.

links.label: Where this internalized rule gets tested hardest

entries.title: A body horror scene deliberately meant to unsettle, not thrill
entries.body: Anno has said outright he wanted the sight of Eva-01 devouring Zeruel to disturb young viewers, even make a child vomit, arguing that sex and violence are ordinary parts of life and that shielding children from "repulsive things" does them no favors. Scholars have read the scene in sharply different directions since — as an act coded feminine and maternal (Eva-01 build from Lilith, folding a "sibling" Angel born of Adam into itself) as much as it is monstrous.

links.label: The scene this reading is built on

entries.title: Shinji dissolves into Eva-01's cockpit
entries.body: In the aftermath of the Zeruel fight, Shinji's body dissolves inside Unit-01's cockpit; NERV spends a month devising a recovery plan while Shinji, without a physical body, drifts through an extended reconstruction of his own memories and motivations for piloting at all.

links.label: The battle this follows directly
The equivalent clip-show/monologue structure from episode 14

entries.scene: Shinji, dissolved inside the Eva, senses Yui and is breastfed as an infant in his own memory
entries.title: "Anywhere can be heaven if you have the desire to live"
entries.body: The episode's title references Freud's oral stage, the earliest phase of psychosexual development centered on the mother's breast; Shinji's dissolution inside Eva-01 is staged explicitly around nursing and womb imagery, and it's Yui's presence — not Gendo's, not Misato's — that ultimately persuades him to choose to return to his body at all, repeating a line ("anywhere can be heaven if you have the desire to live") that recurs almost verbatim in The End of Evangelion.

links.label: The theory this scene is the strongest evidence for
The earlier "good breast/bad breast" reading this directly echoes

entries.scene: The episode's closing scene, implying Misato and Kaji have sex
entries.title: An implied sex scene that provoked real backlash
entries.body: The episode closes on an implied, non-explicit sex scene between Misato and Kaji, aired in a supposedly protected evening timeslot; it drew immediate controversy in Japan as unsuitable for a show watched by children, and producer Toshimichi Ōtsuki — who by that point had largely stopped being consulted on the show day-to-day — has said he'd have stopped it if he'd seen it before broadcast. Anno has defended it on the same grounds he's used elsewhere: that shielding children from sex and violence does them no favors.

links.label: Back to Kaji
The wider critical debate over the show's sexual content

entries.scene: SEELE interrogates a kidnapped Fuyutsuki about his past with Gendo
entries.title: Fuyutsuki's flashback: Yui, Gendo, and the founding of Gehirn
entries.body: Under interrogation, Fuyutsuki recalls falling for a young researcher, Yui Ikari — then still involved with a man using his old surname, Rokubungi — while growing suspicious that Gendo was really after her connections to SEELE. Investigating Second Impact and an artificial cavity in Antarctica leads Fuyutsuki straight to Gendo and SEELE's involvement; shown the full scope of the Evangelion project by Gendo and researcher Naoko Akagi, he joins the organization that will later become NERV.

links.label: Back to Gendo
The disaster Fuyutsuki was investigating

entries.title: Yui's death, in Fuyutsuki's own account
entries.body: In 2004, Yui dies volunteering as the subject of a contact experiment with the newly built Evangelion Unit-01 — the flashback's most direct on-screen account of how she died, though it stops short of confirming what happened to her afterward. Gendo, after a period of mourning, is the one who then proposes the Human Instrumentality Project to Fuyutsuki.

links.label: The theory of what happened to her next
The project Gendo proposes right after

entries.scene: Naoko finds the first Rei clone alone and lost inside Gehirn's base
entries.title: Naoko strangles the first Rei, then takes her own life
entries.body: After completing the Magi, Naoko finds the newly created first Rei clone wandering Gehirn's base; when the girl echoes something cruel Gendo apparently called Naoko, and Naoko recognizes Yui's features in Rei's face, she strangles the child and then kills herself. Gehirn is restructured and renamed NERV in the aftermath.

links.label: Ritsuko's own relationship with Naoko
The clone lineage this death sits inside
The system Naoko had just finished

entries.title: White Moon and Black Moon
entries.body: Fuyutsuki's investigation surfaces two giant artificial cavities: one beneath Antarctica (White Moon) and one beneath Hakone, under what becomes NERV's geofront (Black Moon) — both said to have arrived on Earth during a prehistoric "Giant Impact" carried out by an alien First Ancestral Race. The concept is only sketched here; a video game spin-off later fleshes out the idea that the Black Moon carried Lilith to Earth in the first place.

links.label: The city built over the Black Moon's location
The prehistoric event this cavity is tied to

entries.scene: SEELE's members are visualized as identical black monoliths during Fuyutsuki's interrogation
entries.title: SEELE's monolith imagery, borrowed from 2001: A Space Odyssey
entries.body: SEELE's members are depicted, for the first time, as a row of featureless black monoliths rather than people — a direct visual reference to the monoliths of Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (and, behind that, Arthur C. Clarke's short story "The Sentinel"), reinforcing SEELE's fixation on forcing the next stage of human evolution.

links.label: Back to SEELE
The evolutionary leap SEELE is forcing

entries.title: Kaji's death is pinned on SEELE
entries.body: Kaji frees the kidnapped Fuyutsuki and is killed immediately afterward. During the episode's original TV broadcast, some viewers suspected Misato was somehow responsible; the later, extended "video format" version re-edited the closing scenes specifically to make clear SEELE's own agents killed him, not Misato.

links.label: The death this confirms the culprit for

entries.scene: Asuka's flashback to her mother Kyoko's decline and suicide
entries.title: Kyoko Zeppelin Souryuu's madness and death
entries.body: Asuka's mother Kyoko developed a severe mental illness after her own contact experiment with an Evangelion unit, eventually coming to treat a doll as if it were her daughter while the real Asuka watched, before dying by suicide — with Asuka present, and refusing to cry at the funeral afterward. Part of Kyoko's psyche is implied to remain bound up in the Evangelion unit she made contact with, echoing the pattern already established with Yui and Unit-01.

links.label: Back to Asuka
The parallel mother-in-the-Eva theory
A parallel mother's breakdown, one generation over

entries.scene: Arael attacks Asuka's mind directly with a beam of light rather than fighting Eva-02
entries.title: Arael's psychological attack on Asuka
entries.body: Rather than fighting conventionally, the Angel Arael erodes Asuka's psyche directly through a beam of light, forcing her repressed memories of her mother's breakdown and death to the surface and leaving her unable to function as a pilot afterward. Critics have described the sequence in terms as strong as "mind rape," and it's the first of several Angels in the back half of the series to attack psychologically rather than physically.

links.label: The memories this attack forces to the surface
What this kind of attack implies about the Angels

entries.scene: Gendo orders the Spear of Longinus fired into lunar orbit to stop Arael
entries.title: The Spear is fired at the Moon — and SEELE loses it
entries.body: To defeat Arael, Gendo has Unit-00 extract the Spear of Longinus from the crucified figure in Terminal Dogma and launch it into lunar orbit, over Fuyutsuki's and Misato's objections. The move works, but it also permanently strips SEELE of a weapon central to its own version of Instrumentality — making unmistakably clear that Gendo is running his own, incompatible agenda underneath NERV's.

links.label: How the Spear got to Terminal Dogma in the first place
The plan this weapon was meant to serve
The figure the Spear is pulled from

entries.scene: Asuka and Rei are left alone together in an elevator for nearly a full minute of silence
entries.title: The elevator scene, and Asuka calling Rei a "doll"
entries.body: An unusually long, nearly motionless freeze-frame leaves Asuka and Rei alone in an elevator; when Rei finally suggests Asuka simply isn't opening her heart to Unit-02, Asuka calls her a "doll" and slaps her. Critics have singled the scene out both as a striking use of stillness and as thematically central — Rei's insistence, later in the episode, that she isn't a doll either complicates Asuka's accusation directly.

links.label: Back to Rei
Back to Asuka

entries.title: Asuka's collapsing sync ratio is psychological, not physical
entries.body: Misato initially wonders if Asuka's sudden, sharp drop in Eva-02 performance is tied to her first menstrual cycle; Ritsuko argues instead that the real cause is psychological — Asuka's mounting jealousy of Shinji and Rei, and the resurfacing trauma around her mother. Critics have read Asuka's whole arc through this episode as "masculine protest" pushed to its breaking point: a girl who built her entire self-worth on outperforming everyone around her, finally forced to confront that the performance was covering for something else.

links.label: The same masculine-protest reading from episode 11
The trauma underneath the collapse

entries.scene: Armisael penetrates Eva-00 and Rei's mind directly
entries.title: Armisael, and Rei's decision to self-destruct
entries.body: The Angel Armisael attacks by physically penetrating Unit-00 and merging with Rei's own mind rather than fighting conventionally. Unable to dislodge it any other way, Rei chooses to detonate herself along with the Angel inside her own Eva — killing Armisael, destroying a chunk of Tokyo-3, and (seemingly) herself.

links.label: Why her death isn't quite the end of the story
The same kind of psychological attack, one episode earlier

entries.scene: Ritsuko, sent by Gendo to a SEELE interrogation in Rei's place, shows Shinji and Misato the truth
entries.title: Ritsuko exposes — and destroys — Rei's spare clones
entries.body: Furious at being used as Rei's stand-in, Ritsuko takes Shinji and Misato down into Terminal Dogma and reveals what NERV has kept hidden: a tank of soulless, replaceable Rei clones, only one of which is ever "active" at a time. Out of anger at Gendo, Ritsuko destroys the remaining clones on the spot, then breaks down in tears.

links.label: The clone tank this confirms
Ritsuko's own history with betrayal and motherhood

entries.scene: The newly awakened Rei III finds Gendo's old glasses, kept by her predecessor since episode 1
entries.title: The new Rei tries to break the old Rei's attachment — and can't quite do it
entries.body: Rei III attempts to break the spare pair of Gendo's glasses her predecessor had kept and guarded since the very first episode — then stops and cries instead, an unscripted-feeling crack in the idea that each new Rei starts as a blank slate. Anno has said the new clone still carries the previous one's memories, and reads the scene as Rei III trying, and failing, to fully sever the emotional tie the earlier Rei had to Gendo.

links.label: The scene, back in episode 5, where those glasses first mattered
The larger question of how much carries over between clones

entries.scene: Armisael, after failing with Rei, tries to merge with Shinji's Eva-01 instead
entries.title: Armisael's proposal echoes Rei's own buried wish
entries.body: After Rei subdues it, Armisael turns and tries to "become one" with Shinji's Unit-01 instead — nearly the same words used during Shinji's own dissolution into Eva-01 three episodes earlier. Rei recognizes, in the moment, that Armisael's move mirrors an unconscious desire of her own to merge with Shinji; it's presented as part of what finally pushes her toward her decision to self-destruct rather than let the Angel take him instead.

links.label: The earlier scene this echoes almost verbatim
Where this realization leads her

entries.title: Asuka drops out entirely
entries.body: Following Arael's psychic attack, Asuka sinks into what the episode frames as clinical depression: she moves out of Misato's apartment into her friend Hikari's, stops engaging with anyone, and spends her days playing video games instead. It's the most visible sign yet of how completely her earlier confidence has collapsed.

links.label: The breakdown this follows directly

entries.title: Originally "The Human Instrumentality Project" — and a decision the staff came to regret
entries.body: This episode was originally titled "The Human Instrumentality Project" in Gainax's 1993 planning document, envisioned as a dense reveal of Gendo's and Ritsuko's true intentions, with the next episode meant to bring twelve powerful new Angels down from the Moon. Series assistant director Kazuya Tsurumaki has said he initially opposed killing off the second Rei this late in the series, and staff — Tsurumaki included — have since said they regretted not giving Rei II's specific personality more room before replacing her.

links.label: The project this episode was originally going to be named for
Another early plan abandoned partway through production

entries.title: A dry, fast-paced reveal episode — reviewers split on the execution
entries.body: "Rei III" drew a 6.9% rating and split critics: some praised the starkness of Rei's true nature finally being spelled out and the intensity of the Armisael battle, while others felt the reveal wasted a stronger character concept by resolving it so quickly, and criticized recycled animation and some of the voice performances.

entries.scene: Kaworu descends into Terminal Dogma expecting to find Adam
entries.title: Kaworu discovers the giant is Lilith, not Adam — and stops
entries.body: Sent by SEELE to reach the being kept in Terminal Dogma, Kaworu finds it's actually Lilith, not Adam as he (and everyone else) had assumed. Recognizing humanity's will to live, he abandons the mission entirely and asks Shinji to kill him instead — the same Adam/Lilith mix-up that has run through the whole series, this time settled at the cost of Kaworu's own life.

links.label: The figure Kaworu finds instead of Adam
The wider pattern of Adam/Lilith mix-ups this resolves
What this decision meant for him personally

entries.scene: Kaworu explains the AT Field to Shinji
entries.title: "The walls of the heart"
entries.body: Kaworu describes the AT Field — introduced purely as a combat mechanic back in episode 1 — as the barrier separating one person's heart from everyone else's. Rather than attacking Shinji's defenses the way earlier Angels did, Kaworu lowers them through kindness instead; the show's own staff have said the AT Field carried no such philosophical weight when it was first written, and only became "walls of the heart" retroactively, here.

links.label: The concept's original, purely mechanical introduction
The larger project built on dissolving these same walls

entries.title: A much more explicit draft, and a director who nearly quit
entries.body: Screenwriter Akio Satsukawa's original script for this episode was considerably more overtly homoerotic — including a scene of Shinji and Kaworu swimming naked together and kissing. Anno found it too explicit and rewrote it, relocating the intimacy to NERV's public baths instead; episode director Masayuki has said he seriously considered walking off the production over the content in Satsukawa's draft.

links.label: The ambiguity this rewrite still leaves in place

entries.title: The one episode with no original score
