entries.body: Unlike every other episode, this one uses no music by series composer Shirō Sagisu at all — its only accompaniment is Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, specifically the "Ode to Joy," which Kaworu hums on first meeting Shinji and which later plays under both his death and the episode's climactic battle.

links.label: The recurring closing-theme pattern this episode alone skips

entries.scene: The episode closes on an extended still image of Kaworu cradled in Eva-01's hand
entries.title: A held frame, timed to the length of Kaworu's death
entries.body: The episode ends on roughly a minute-long still shot of Kaworu in Unit-01's palm — the same held-frame technique the show had already used for tense character moments in episodes 4 and 22, here stretched out for the full length of Shinji's hesitation before he finally kills him.

links.label: The earlier long freeze-frame this technique echoes

entries.title: "I love you" becomes "I like you"
entries.body: Netflix's 2019 English redub changed Kaworu's line to Shinji from ADV's earlier "I love you" to "I like you," and "worthy of love" to "worthy of grace" — a change some fans read as queer erasure. The new translator has defended the choice as closer to the ambiguity of the original Japanese suki, and Shinji's own Japanese voice actress, Megumi Ogata, publicly said she'd always read the line the same way and welcomed the revision.

links.label: The underlying ambiguity both translations are wrestling with

entries.title: One of the series' most acclaimed episodes
entries.body: This episode topped the 1997 Animage readers' poll for best episode of the year, with Kaworu placing second in the same poll's best-male-character category. Western critical reception has been just as strong, though Kaworu's introduction and his relationship with Shinji have remained a subject of extensive debate among both scholars and fans.

entries.title: Who actually wrote each episode
entries.body: Per Anime News Network's staff credits, script duties break down as: Hideaki Anno on every episode except the fourth (episodes 1–3 and 5–26), Akio Satsukawa co-credited on 12 of those, Yōji Enokido on episodes 2, 7, 8, and 11, Hiroshi Yamaguchi on episodes 16, 22, and 23, Shinji Higuchi on episodes 17 and 18, and Mitsuo Iso as the sole writer of episode 13. Episode 4, "Hedgehog's Dilemma," is the only one of the 26 with no Anno script credit at all.

links.label: The one episode Anno didn't personally script
Iso's episode, written solo
Satsukawa's original, more explicit draft of episode 24

entries.title: Who actually storyboarded and directed each episode
entries.body: Beyond Anno's overall series direction, per-episode storyboard and "episode director" credits (as distinct roles) were spread across a rotating team: Kazuya Tsurumaki and Masayuki each handled roughly six to eight episodes; Hiroyuki Ishido about five. Several episodes have specific, named episode directors: Tsuyoshi Kaga (4, 10), Keiichi Sugiyama (5, 7), Seiji Mizushima (9), Tetsuya Watanabe (11), Tensai Okamura (13), Ken Andō and Masahiko Ōtsuka (14), Naoyasu Habu (15), Minoru Ōhara (17), Akira Takamura (22), Shōichi Masuo (23), and Masayuki himself on 19, 24, and 26 — the finale.

links.label: The director/writer split, back in episode 1
Okamura's episode
Masayuki's episode 19

entries.title: The Japanese voice cast, and a few of its stranger double-castings
entries.body: Core cast: Megumi Ogata (Shinji), Megumi Hayashibara (Rei Ayanami — and also Yui Ikari), Kotono Mitsuishi (Misato), Yūko Miyamura (Asuka), Fumihiko Tachiki (Gendo), Yuriko Yamaguchi (Ritsuko), Kōichi Yamadera (Kaji), Motomu Kiyokawa (Fuyutsuki), Akira Ishida (Kaworu, episode 24), Mugihito (Keel Lorenz), Tomokazu Seki (Toji), Tetsuya Iwanaga (Kensuke), Junko Iwao (Hikari), and Miki Nagasawa (Maya). Per Anime News Network's cast credits, Hayashibara is also billed as the voice of "EVA-01 (Berserker)" — meaning the same actress who voices Rei and Yui is the one making Unit-01's inhuman berserk-state sounds, a small but suggestive piece of casting given the theories about whose soul is actually driving the Eva in those moments.

links.label: The theory this casting choice quietly supports
The berserk state being voiced
Back to Rei

entries.title: Nearly every episode ends with a different cover of "Fly Me to the Moon"
entries.body: Rather than reusing one closing theme recording, the series pairs Bart Howard's "Fly Me to the Moon" with a new arrangement and vocalist almost every episode — sung in turn by Claire, Yoko Takahashi, and, in character-specific versions, by Megumi Hayashibara as Rei, Yūko Miyamura as Asuka, and Kotono Mitsuishi as Misato (sometimes all three together), plus a couple of purely instrumental versions by composer Shirō Sagisu himself. Episode 24 is the one conspicuous exception, using no version of the song at all — consistent with it being the only episode built entirely around Beethoven's Ninth instead.

links.label: The episode that breaks this pattern entirely

entries.title: Asuka Langley Souryuu
entries.body: A German-Japanese prodigy pilot whose relentless competitiveness is a defense mechanism built on childhood trauma (her mother's breakdown and suicide). Her arc tracks what happens when a self-worth built entirely on being needed as a pilot stops working.

links.label: Her first on-screen appearance
Her first fight alongside Shinji

entries.title: Ryoji Kaji
entries.body: Officially a NERV agent, unofficially reporting to SEELE and Japan's government simultaneously, digging into NERV's secrets — including Adam and Instrumentality — while romantically entangled with Misato.

links.label: The secret he keeps digging into
What that digging costs him
Escorting Asuka to Japan
His unresolved history with Misato
What he shows Misato in Terminal Dogma

entries.title: Studio Ghibli animated this one
entries.body: Episode 11 — the MAGI-computer-meltdown, power-outage bottle episode — was farmed out to Studio Ghibli staff as a contracted production. It shows: the art style, character expressions, and tone come out noticeably more comedic and warm than the episodes around it.

links.label: The other studios that quietly worked on individual episodes

quote.original: グロス請け担当プロダクションの違いによる画風の差もあり、スタジオジブリのスタッフが担当した第拾壱話は、絵柄だけでなくキャラ描写や話の展開もコミカルでポジティブなものになっている。
quote.translation: "There are also differences in art style due to which contracted production studio handled a given episode — episode 11, handled by Studio Ghibli staff, comes out comedic and positive not just in its linework but in its character portrayal and story beats."

entries.title: MAGI
entries.body: NERV's supercomputer system: three semi-independent processors — Casper, Melchior, and Balthasar, named for the Biblical Three Magi — modeled on different aspects of their designer Naoko Akagi's personality, which must reach consensus to authorize NERV's most critical decisions.

links.label: The Magi's biggest on-screen test
What the three-way split is read as symbolizing

quote.original: NERV本部には「カスパー（CASPER）」「メルキオール（MELCHIOR）」「バルタザール（BALTHASAR）」の3つから構成されるオリジナルが設置されている。この三つのスーパーコンピュータの名前はイエス・キリストが誕生した時に東方からきた三賢者の名前である。
quote.translation: "NERV headquarters houses the original system, composed of three units: Casper, Melchior, and Balthasar. These three supercomputers are named after the Three Wise Men who came from the East at the birth of Jesus Christ."

entries.scene: Episode title translates literally as "SEELE, Seat of the Soul"
entries.title: SEELE
entries.body: A secretive committee that founded NERV and steers events from behind it, working from the Dead Sea Scrolls toward its own version of the Human Instrumentality Project — a version Gendo Ikari is simultaneously trying to hijack for himself.

links.label: The text they're both working from
The shell-company front SEELE's members hide behind
The symbolism behind SEELE's own emblem
How SEELE's members are actually shown on-screen

quote.original: ゼーレ（SEELE） - NERVの上部組織とされる秘密結社。
quote.translation: "SEELE — a secret society said to be NERV's parent organization."

entries.title: What do the Dead Sea Scrolls actually say?
entries.body: SEELE and NERV both act on a text called the Dead Sea Scrolls that supposedly predicts the Angels' attacks and the path to Instrumentality. Its actual contents are never shown or quoted at length.

quote.original: 裏死海文書 - ゼーレが所持する預言書。
quote.translation: "The (Hidden) Dead Sea Scrolls — a prophetic text held by SEELE."

entries.title: The episode almost nobody saw live
entries.body: TV Tokyo bumped this episode to a New Year's Day 8:30am slot (instead of its normal Wednesday 6:30pm one) to make room for New Year's programming. The result was a 0.9% household rating — the lowest of the entire series, versus the finale's series-high 10.3%. Producers had anticipated the dip: a clip-show recap originally slotted for episode 14 was swapped with this episode instead, so the low-visibility slot fell on new content rather than a recap.

quote.original: 第拾四話のテレビ東京での放映分については、1月3日という放送日の都合（テレビ東京が本来の放送時間に正月特番を放送した）により、同日午前8時30分からの放映...当初は第拾参話に予定されていた総集編を第拾四話と入れ替えて製作・放送された。
quote.translation: "Episode 14's TV Tokyo broadcast, owing to the circumstances of its January 3rd air date (TV Tokyo aired New Year's specials in its usual broadcast slot), aired instead from 8:30am that same day... the recap episode originally scheduled for episode 13 was swapped with episode 14 and produced/broadcast in that order."

entries.scene: Power cable severed, plug depth critical — it keeps fighting anyway
entries.title: Unit-01's unpowered "berserk" state
entries.body: Unit-01 keeps fighting an Angel after its power cable is severed and its plug depth goes critical — something no dummy plug or external system explains. The show treats this as evidence the Eva itself is, in some sense, alive.

links.label: One reading of why
The forced-override system this isn't
The earliest hint of this, back in episode 2
Who actually voices this state

entries.title: Yui's soul inside Unit-01
entries.body: The show never states in dialogue that Yui Ikari's soul resides in Unit-01, but strongly implies it — her disappearance during an activation test, Gendo's fixation on the unit, and Unit-01's unpowered "berserk" rescues of Shinji are the load-bearing evidence. Anno has confirmed the broader mechanism in interviews (a pilot syncs with an Evangelion "through their mother's soul," an idea he traces to an NHK documentary on the brain), which lends real weight to the reading — but the specific claim that it's Yui's soul in Unit-01 is still never said outright on-screen.

links.label: Where that ambiguity comes to a head
The earliest staging that hints at this
An early unexplained rampage this could explain
The equivalent mother-in-the-machine reading for Ritsuko
The contact experiment that killed her
A casting detail that quietly backs up this theory

quote.original: 母親の魂を介すことでEVAとシンクロする。この設定は、NHKスペシャル『驚異の小宇宙 人体II 脳と心』から着想を得ている。
quote.translation: "[A pilot] syncs with an Evangelion by way of their mother's soul. This idea was inspired by the NHK Special documentary 'Wonders of the Micro-Cosmos: The Human Body II — Brain and Mind.'"

entries.scene: Gendo forces Unit-01 onto autopilot to destroy the Angel-possessed Unit-03
entries.title: The Dummy System (autonomous override)
entries.body: Distinct from the dummy plug used later in the mass-production Evas: this is an autonomous control system Gendo activates on Unit-01 itself, overriding Shinji's control entirely to destroy Unit-03 — which the 13th Angel has taken over — without Shinji's consent. Only afterward does Shinji learn his own friend, Toji Suzuhara, was in Unit-03's cockpit, maimed by his own Eva's hands. It's what finally makes Shinji quit piloting, right up until the next Angel attack forces his hand again.

links.label: The related but distinct mass-production system
Back to Shinji
Back to Toji's introduction

quote.original: ゲンドウはEVAの自律型操縦システム「ダミーシステム」を起動させる。シンジの意思とは無関係に初号機は3号機を破壊し、コックピット（エントリープラグ）を握り潰す。そしてシンジは、そこに自分の友人、鈴原トウジが乗っていたことを知る。
quote.translation: "Gendo activates the Eva's autonomous control system, the 'Dummy System.' Independent of Shinji's will, Unit-01 destroys Unit-03 and crushes its cockpit (entry plug). Shinji then learns that his own friend, Toji Suzuhara, had been piloting it."

entries.scene: The mass-production Evangelions are activated
entries.title: Dummy plug system
entries.body: An unmanned-operation system meant to let an Evangelion fight without a live pilot, built by transplanting a simulated version of a pilot's mental patterns into the entry plug — Rei's for Unit-00's dummy plug, and Kaworu's for the nine mass-production Evangelions (Units 05 through 13).

links.label: How much of a person is really in there
The related but distinct Unit-01 override

quote.original: 5-13号機　MASS PRODUCTION MODEL　ホワイト　ダミープラグ
quote.translation: "Units 5–13, Mass Production Model, white, [piloted by the] Dummy Plug." (from the series' Evangelion-units table)

entries.title: Human Instrumentality Project
entries.body: The plan, pursued in incompatible versions by SEELE and by Gendo, to trigger a forced next stage of human evolution by dissolving every individual AT Field and merging all souls into one, via a ritual called the Third Impact.

links.label: The ritual that carries it out

quote.original: 人類補完計画 - NERV、ゼーレが極秘で進めている謎の計画。
quote.translation: "The Human Instrumentality Project — a mysterious plan being secretly advanced by NERV and SEELE."

entries.scene: Kaji lays out what the Katsuragi Expedition really did
entries.title: Adam
entries.body: The first of the beings created by the "First Ancestral Race" long before humanity; the Angels are described as Adam's offspring. A contact experiment on Adam is what triggered Second Impact.

links.label: Adam vs. Lilith, precisely which is which
The two artificial cavities tied to Adam's and Lilith's arrival

quote.original: 第1使徒　アダム　使徒を生み出した生命の起源の一つ。セカンドインパクトを引き起こした。
quote.translation: "1st Angel: Adam — one of the two origins of life that gave rise to the Angels. Triggered Second Impact."

entries.title: What was First Impact?
entries.body: Referenced as the event that shaped the Earth long before Second Impact, tied to Adam and Lilith's arrival. Different tie-in material describes it differently, and the TV series itself barely touches it.

entries.scene: Fuyutsuki is pressed on what Gendo is really after
entries.title: Gendo as tragic rather than purely villainous
entries.body: Gendo's plan is explicitly framed here as wanting to be with Yui again, but how much sympathy that deserves given the harm he causes Shinji and everyone around him to get there is a matter of ongoing viewer disagreement rather than something the text adjudicates for you.

links.label: Back to Gendo's introduction
How Gendo and Yui's relationship actually started

entries.scene: Misato takes Shinji down into Terminal Dogma
entries.title: Lilith
entries.body: A being of the same origin as Adam, kept crucified and sealed in NERV's Terminal Dogma. The Lilin — i.e., humanity — are described as descended from Lilith rather than Adam, and Lilith's flesh and soul are the source material for the Evangelions and for Rei.

links.label: Her connection to Rei
Which of these two is which, again?
The other artifact kept in the same chamber
The scene where Kaji first shows her off, misidentified
The Spear being pulled out of her and fired at the Moon
Where the name Lilith comes from, outside the show

entries.title: Lilith, outside Evangelion: Adam's rejected first partner
entries.body: In Jewish folklore, Lilith is Adam's first partner, made — unlike Eve — from the same dirt as Adam himself; she refuses subordination to him and is cast out, after which Mesopotamian tradition attaches to her name a whole class of demons blamed for promiscuity and child-snatching, and some sources give her a subsequent romance with Samael, the archangel of death. More recent retellings have recast her as a symbol of independent womanhood rather than a monster. The show's own Lilith keeps the "origin of humanity, treated as something to be used" thread from the myth, but drops the demonic and vampiric associations the name usually carries elsewhere in pop culture.

links.label: The being this name belongs to in the show
Where her "children," humanity, land on NERV's own Angel list

entries.title: Adam/Lilith identity mix-ups across versions
entries.body: Which being is sealed in Terminal Dogma, which one Gendo's faction actually possesses, and which one the embryo NERV keeps separately is called is inconsistent enough between the TV series, supplementary material, and later reprints that fans still debate the "correct" mapping. Some treat this as evidence of a deliberately unresolved cosmology rather than a continuity error.

entries.title: Kaji is killed
entries.body: Kaji is killed off-screen in this episode, having gotten too close to the truth about Adam, Lilith, and Instrumentality he'd spent the series digging into. Who specifically killed him (SEELE or Gendo's own faction) is left unstated.

links.label: Back to Kaji's introduction
The later edit that confirms who actually did it

quote.original: 一方、廃人状態であったアスカは目を覚まし...（第22話の文脈で加持がその死の直前まで調査を続けていたことが描かれる）
quote.translation: "Meanwhile Asuka, who had been catatonic, awakens..." (the episode's synopsis places Kaji's death here, mid-way through NERV's occupation crisis, after his investigation into NERV's secrets)

entries.scene: The mass-production Evangelions are activated
entries.title: How much of a person is in a dummy plug
entries.body: The dummy plug is described as simulating a pilot's mental patterns rather than containing a true digitized soul, but the mass-production Evas' dummy plugs are built from Kaworu specifically, and their on-screen behavior (screaming, bleeding) reads as more than simulation. How much of that is meant literally is left to the viewer.

links.label: The Kaworu these are built from

entries.title: The Rei clones
entries.body: A tank of spare Rei bodies is kept in Terminal Dogma; when a given Rei dies, another takes her place, personality and memory carried over to a degree the show never fully explains.

links.label: Whether that's really "her"

entries.title: Lilith's soul divided across Rei and Unit-00
entries.body: Building on a scene in The End of Evangelion where Rei is welcomed "home" by Lilith, a popular theory holds that souls in this universe are divisible, and that a fragment of Lilith's soul persists in each Rei clone and possibly in Unit-00 itself (offered as one explanation for Unit-00's own unexplained hostile incidents). This is an inference from a handful of suggestive scenes, not a stated rule.

links.label: The scene this theory is built on
The earliest hint of this, well before it's explained

entries.title: Do the Rei clones share one continuous identity?
entries.body: Each Rei carries the prior one's memories to some extent, but the show never states whether that makes her the same person, a new person with inherited memories, or something in between — the question is posed to the audience more than once and never answered for them.

entries.title: Kaworu Nagisa
entries.body: Arrives late in the story as a new pilot candidate, forms an immediate bond with Shinji, and is then revealed to be an Angel in human form, sent by SEELE to reach Lilith in Terminal Dogma. Shinji is left to decide whether to kill him.

links.label: What he actually felt
Is he really an Angel, though?

entries.title: What Kaworu actually felt for Shinji
entries.body: Kaworu tells Shinji he loves him within a day of meeting him, then lets Shinji kill him rather than fight back. Whether this is genuine affection an Angel is nonetheless capable of, a calculated move to complete his mission, or both at once, is never resolved — the scene is written to support any of the three.

entries.title: Is Kaworu an Angel, in exactly the same sense the others are?
entries.body: Kaworu is called the Seventeenth Angel but presents as fully human and self-aware in a way none of the others do, and material outside the original TV run has described his origin differently. The TV series itself leaves the discrepancy alone.

links.label: Where humanity itself lands on the same numbered list
Why his Angel name alone breaks from every other Angel's naming pattern

entries.title: Tabris: the one Angel name with no "god" in it
entries.body: Every other Angel's name is built by theophory — tacking a form of "-el" (god) onto a root word. Tabris (Kaworu's Angel name) breaks that pattern outright; it traces instead to the occult text The Nuctemeron, attributed to Apollonius of Tyana, which names Tabris the "genius of free will" and ruler of the sixth hour, glossed by 19th-century magician Éliphas Lévi as "the magus is free; he is the occult king of the earth" — language that lines up closely with the freedom Kaworu tries to hand Shinji. A separate, likely-unrelated tradition gives a woman named Tharbis (or Tabris) as a wife Moses later uses a memory-erasing pair of rings to leave behind, a story some read as a loose echo of Shinji and Kaworu's own short-lived, deliberately incomplete bond.

links.label: The naming pattern every other Angel follows
The wider ambiguity around what Kaworu actually is
The relationship this mythology is read against

entries.scene: Rei and Kaworu both project AT Fields here without any on-screen core or S² organ
entries.title: Do Rei and Kaworu even have S² organs?
entries.body: A later addition to the same forum thread raises a wrinkle in the soul-driven-core theory: both Rei and Kaworu project AT Fields in this episode, and NERV's own dialogue elsewhere ties AT Field generation to S²-scale power, yet neither shows any sign of a core or S² organ the way Adam-derived Angels and Evas do. Suggested fixes floated on the thread include a separate, core-free "S² effect" available only to Lilith-derived bodies, or an angelic soul temporarily switching on some latent Lilim capacity — but posters concede neither is confirmed by anything the show actually shows.

links.label: The soul/core theory this complicates
The mechanic this AT Field use is measured against
The wider ambiguity around what Kaworu even is

entries.scene: The episode's Japanese title
entries.title: The title "最後のシ者" is a pun
entries.body: The Japanese title for this episode splits the kanji in Kaworu's surname, Nagisa (渚), into its component radicals and re-renders one as the katakana シ, so the title reads as "the last シ者" — deliberately ambiguous between 使者 ("messenger," SEELE's errand for Kaworu) and 死者 ("the dead," what he becomes by the end of it).

links.label: The Kaworu this refers to

quote.original: 「シ者」は、渚カヲルの「渚」の偏と旁を分けたもの。使者、あるいは死者。
quote.translation: "'シ者' is formed by splitting the radical and phonetic components of Kaworu Nagisa's surname kanji, 渚. [It reads ambiguously as] 使者 ('messenger'), or 死者 ('the dead')."

entries.title: Acceptance vs. rejection of Instrumentality
entries.body: A common reading pairs the TV finale and The End of Evangelion as two sides of the same choice: the TV ending shows Shinji arriving at self-acceptance from inside a dissolved, unified consciousness, while EoE shows the same decision played out physically — Shinji ultimately rejecting total union with others in favor of a painful but individual existence. Neither film states this framing outright; it's inferred from how the two versions rhyme.

links.label: Why there are two endings at all
How EoE actually plays it out

entries.scene: The finale breaks into congratulatory character-actor cutaways
entries.title: The finale as commentary on Anno's own depression
entries.body: Director Hideaki Anno has spoken about depression during the show's production, and the TV finale's abrupt turn toward real-world footage, character-actor congratulations, and direct address to the viewer is widely read as breaking the fourth wall on purpose — a message about escapism versus engaging with a difficult reality, layered on top of Shinji's in-story arc rather than replacing it. Sociologist Miyadai Shinji has argued the series itself started as a lighter, more conventional "school anime" concept and drifted toward this ending as production wore on and the director's own state of mind changed.

links.label: The same self-scrutiny, voiced during episode 1

quote.original: 庵野は「人間ドラマは頭の中で考えてもできないので、仕方なく自分をドラマにそのまま投影しており、『エヴァ』のキャラは全部自分自身だというのはそういう意味だ」と語っている。
quote.translation: "Anno has said: 'I can't write human drama just by thinking it up in my head, so I end up projecting myself directly into the drama instead — that's what I mean when I say every character in Eva is really myself.'"

entries.title: "I mustn't run away" becomes "it's okay to run away"
entries.body: Shinji's early refrain — "I mustn't run away" (逃げちゃダメだ) — is the closest thing the show has to a stated thesis in its first half. By the finale it's been replaced with the opposite: it's okay to run away. Character designer Yoshiyuki Sadamoto is credited with suggesting the shift.

links.label: How that plays out differently in EoE
Where the original line actually comes from
The first dry run of running away, back in episode 4

quote.original: 物語開始直後に「逃げちゃダメだ」と言っていたのが、最後に「逃げてもいい」に変わったのは、貞本のアドバイスによる。
quote.translation: "That the line 'I mustn't run away,' spoken right at the story's start, changed to 'it's okay to run away' by the end, came from [character designer Yoshiyuki] Sadamoto's suggestion."

entries.title: Why did the finale turn out this way? Even the staff disagree
entries.body: The standard explanation is that production had fallen catastrophically behind — only around a third of the episodes were fully animated by the time the show started airing, and the two finale episodes were assembled largely from recycled footage out of necessity. But several staff accounts complicate that: magazine editor Ogura Yuichiro says the finale's plot points were already locked in by January 1996, two months before broadcast; GAINAX president Yamaga Hiroyuki says the show was never so broken it couldn't have been finished conventionally; and assistant director Tsurumaki Kazuya has said Anno had "a chance of winning" with this ending in mind from the start, and considered the backlash itself part of that win — a show forgotten in six months was the actual failure state he was avoiding. Anno himself maintains the finale was always intended to be exactly this, schedule aside, aiming at what he called "liberation from cel animation."

links.label: The other ending this led to
How far behind production already was at episode 1

quote.original: 鶴巻和哉は「第25、26話も庵野監督なりに勝算があってやっている...本当はもっと早い段階で種明かしのネタを全部考えてシナリオを書いちゃうのが一番楽なんですよ。でも庵野監督はそれでは楽しすぎだとか思ったんでしょう」と証言している。
quote.translation: "Tsurumaki Kazuya has testified: 'Episodes 25 and 26 were made with director Anno believing, in his own way, that he had a chance of winning... The easiest thing would really have been to work out every twist far earlier and just write the script. But I think Director Anno felt that would have been too easy, or too enjoyable, [to be the right choice].'"

entries.title: Death & Rebirth, the precursor film
entries.body: Before The End of Evangelion released, Gainax put out Neon Genesis Evangelion: Death & Rebirth (March 1997): its first half, Death, recaps the TV series' first 24 episodes; its second, Rebirth, is a 25-minute preview of what became The End of Evangelion, cutting off right as the Eva Series begins its assault on Unit-02. The full alternate ending only released four months later, in July 1997.

links.label: Why an alternate ending exists at all
The wholly-new film this was originally meant to replace

entries.title: Where "Air" and "Sincerely Yours" come from
entries.body: "Air," the film's first half, is named after the second movement of Bach's Orchestral Suite No. 3 — "Air on the G String" — used in one of its key scenes. "Sincerely Yours," the second half's Japanese title (まごころを、君に), is a tribute to the 1968 film Charly (based on Flowers for Algernon), which was released in Japan under that exact title — continuing a Gainax tradition of naming a series' final installment after an existing story or film.

entries.scene: The Japanese Strategic Self-Defense Force storms NERV headquarters
entries.title: SEELE frames NERV and sends in the military
entries.body: SEELE feeds Japan's government false intelligence branding NERV the real threat to humanity, triggering a military assault on NERV headquarters with orders to kill on sight — a massacre of NERV's own staff. Ritsuko, held for insubordination, is ordered by Gendo to stop SEELE's attempt to hack NERV's MAGI systems; she complies, but had secretly planted a self-destruct command of her own, which fails when the three Magi don't reach unanimous consent — the "Casper" unit, carrying the part of Naoko modeled on her as a woman, votes it down. Gendo shoots Ritsuko dead moments later.

links.label: The mother Casper is modeled on
The three-way split in the Magi this vote depends on
The organization orchestrating the frame-up

entries.scene: Asuka reactivates Eva-02 to fight off the invading forces
entries.title: Asuka's last stand
entries.body: Moved to Unit-02 for safekeeping while catatonic, Asuka overcomes her trauma on learning her dead mother Kyoko's soul is bound up in the Eva itself; she reactivates it and single-handedly destroys the invading military force, then all nine of SEELE's Mass Production Evangelions. The MP units regenerate once Unit-02's power runs out, though, and disembowel it while Shinji — paralyzed in bakelite-sealed Unit-01 — watches, unable to help.

links.label: Kyoko's death and the soul now bound to this Eva
The same soul-in-the-Eva pattern, for Shinji and Yui

entries.scene: Rei rejects Gendo, takes Adam's embryo from his hand, and merges with Lilith
entries.title: Rei's betrayal, and her fusion with Lilith
entries.body: Gendo attempts to merge with Lilith himself, using the Adam embryo he's kept grafted into his own hand, intending to reunite with Yui on his own terms. Rei refuses to let him, takes Adam for herself instead, and merges directly with Lilith — transforming into a colossal version of herself and triggering Third Impact on SEELE's terms rather than Gendo's.

links.label: The being Rei merges with
The soul-splitting theory this scene is read as confirming
Gendo's own version of Instrumentality, denied here

entries.scene: Live-action footage of real streets, cinema audiences, and fan graffiti is intercut into Shinji's Instrumentality sequence
entries.title: Live-action footage as a mirror held up to the audience
entries.body: Anno deliberately broke from animation for parts of the finale, cutting in real film of trains, street lamps, graffiti scrawled on Gainax's own offices, and — most pointedly — footage of a real theater audience watching the previous Evangelion film. Anno has said he wanted something closer to reality than cel animation could give, worried that fans were dissolving their own sense of self into fiction; he called the audience footage itself a kind of mirror, meant to make viewers notice their own reality rather than lose themselves further in his.

links.label: The same fourth-wall-breaking impulse in the TV finale

quote.original: 色々な人たちが過剰にフィクションにのめり込んで、他者が作った脳内世界に自分の存在を依存し過ぎているのが見ていて怖い感じがした。とにかく少しでも外界を認めて、自分の尺度で相対的な視野を持って欲しかった。
quote.translation: "It felt frightening to watch how many people were excessively immersing themselves in fiction, depending too much on a mental world someone else had built for their own sense of existence. I just wanted them, even a little, to acknowledge the outside world and hold onto a relative perspective measured by their own yardstick."

entries.title: Where "kimochi warui" actually came from
entries.body: Asuka's closing line was originally scripted as a colder "I can't stand the idea of being killed by someone like you." Unsatisfied, Anno asked voice actress Yūko Miyamura to imagine waking up to find a stranger had broken in and was masturbating while watching her sleep, then asked what she'd say. Miyamura's genuine, disgusted answer — "kimochi warui" ("how disgusting"/"I feel sick") — became the actual final line of the series.

links.label: The scene this line closes out

quote.original: もし宮村が一人で寝ていて、窓から知らない男が入ってきて、それに気づかず寝ていて、いつでも襲われるような状況だったにもかかわらず、寝ているところを観ながらオナニーされて…それをされたときに目が覚めたらなんて言う？
quote.translation: "Suppose Miyamura were sleeping alone, and an unfamiliar man climbed in through the window — she doesn't notice, she's asleep and vulnerable to attack at any moment — and he masturbates while watching her sleep... if she woke up right as that was happening, what would she say?"

entries.title: A box-office hit, and a fixture on "greatest anime films" lists
entries.body: The End of Evangelion grossed roughly ¥2.47 billion, placed third at the Japanese box office the week it opened (behind The Lost World: Jurassic Park and Princess Mononoke), and won the 1997 Animage Anime Grand Prix along with honors at the Japan Academy Awards and Animation Kobe. It's since been named repeatedly among the greatest animated films ever made, even as its opening masturbation scene and closing strangulation remain among the most argued-over moments in the franchise.

links.label: The ending most argued over

entries.title: The original plan had 28 Angels, not 17
entries.body: Early planning documents describe 28 Angels rather than the 17 the finished show uses, with a climax involving a second wave of 12 Angels descending from the moon alongside Instrumentality's activation. That structural role — a large final wave of antagonists tied to Instrumentality — survives in the finished work in a different form: the nine Mass-Production Evangelions that SEELE deploys near the end.

links.label: The system built into those nine units
The plan they were meant to serve
Another abandoned early draft, from episode 1's own plot

quote.original: 使徒の数が17体ではなく28体であったり、物語のクライマックスでの12使徒との戦いや人類補完計画の発動が含まれていた。
quote.translation: "The number of Angels was 28 rather than 17, and the story's climax was to include a battle against 12 Angels alongside the activation of the Human Instrumentality Project."

entries.title: The wholly-new film that never got made
entries.body: The original 1996 plan was for both replacement final episodes to be an entirely new theatrical film, not a clip-show. Production fell too far behind again; at a February 1997 press conference — one month before the planned release — Anno publicly apologized, and the all-new film was scrapped. What released instead split into two films: a clip-show-plus-new-footage recap (Death (True)²) and then the genuinely new Air/まごころを、君に in July 1997. The original all-new concept became what Japanese sources call a "phantom project" (幻の企画) — never produced in that form.

links.label: Ideas from that scrapped draft
The ending that resulted instead

quote.original: 劇場版の制作が大幅に遅れ、公開1か月前の1997年2月14日に緊急記者会見が開かれた。席上で、庵野秀明総監督が謝罪を行い...同じく夏に公開が予定されていた「完全新作の劇場版」は幻の企画となってしまった。
quote.translation: "Production of the theatrical film fell drastically behind, and an emergency press conference was held on February 14, 1997, one month before release. At it, general director Hideaki Anno apologized... the 'wholly new theatrical film' also planned for that summer became a phantom project."

entries.title: Concepts from the scrapped all-new film
entries.body: Never filmed, so not part of any released continuity — but Anno has described draft ideas from the abandoned all-new film: pilots merging directly with an Evangelion's "womb" rather than using an entry plug, requiring a C-section-like extraction under a strict time limit (missing it meant the pilot's literal death), and Angels that prey on and consume people outright. Anno has noted the latter idea predates, and reads similarly to, Attack on Titan's premise by well over a decade.

links.label: Why this film was never made

quote.original: 「パイロットはエントリープラグを使わずにEVAの子宮に直接入って一体化する」という表現を考えていたという。そして出るときは摘出手術をする。また「タイムリミットがあり、間に合わない場合は取り込まれて『人としては』死んでしまう」という設定だったという。
quote.translation: "They had considered depicting pilots merging directly with an Evangelion's womb without using an entry plug. Getting out again would require a surgical extraction. There was also said to be a time limit — missing it meant being absorbed and dying 'as a human being.'"

entries.title: Two different endings exist
entries.body: The TV series' original episodes 25–26, made under a tightened budget, resolve the story almost entirely inside Shinji's own psyche. The End of Evangelion (1997), a theatrical film, was written and produced afterward as an alternate, effects-driven ending depicting Third Impact's events directly — both are considered canon, telling the same climax from different angles.

links.label: One way to read the pair together

entries.title: Third Impact
entries.body: The series' climax: the event that carries out (or nearly carries out) Human Instrumentality. What actually happens, and how much of it is undone by the end, differs between the TV series' final two episodes and the alternate ending in The End of Evangelion.

links.label: What's left afterward
Does it happen more than once?

entries.scene: Rei III dissolves into Lilith: "I'm home." / "Welcome home."
entries.title: Rei's reunion with Lilith
entries.body: In The End of Evangelion, Rei III is shown reuniting with Lilith with the words "I'm home," and Lilith replying "Welcome home" — one of the few moments the show gestures directly at what Rei actually is.

links.label: The soul-splitting theory this feeds
An earlier apparition read against this scene

entries.scene: The final shot, on the beach
entries.title: What actually happens on the beach at the end of EoE
entries.body: The final shot — Shinji strangling, then stopping, Asuka, who touches his cheek and says "kimochi warui" ("disgusting" / "I feel sick") — is one of anime's most argued-over endings. Readings range from a literal moment between two survivors of a mostly-undone Third Impact, to a purely symbolic beat with no fixed literal status, to a bleak coda implying nothing is resolved. The film gives no voiceover or text to settle it.

links.label: What state the rest of the world is in

entries.title: A cyclical/recurring Third Impact
entries.body: Some fans read hints across the franchise (including the later Rebuild films, which explicitly restart the story after a Third Impact) as evidence that impacts recur in cycles rather than the original TV/EoE story being a one-off — though the original series itself makes no such claim; this reading leans heavily on later material re-interpreted backward.

entries.title: What state is the world actually in after The End of Evangelion?
entries.body: The final scene shows Shinji and Asuka alone on a wrecked shoreline. Whether this is a reversed, near-total, or partial Third Impact — and whether anyone else survived it — is left to the audience.

entries.title: It wasn't just Gainax — and a couple of surprising names show up in the credits
entries.body: Gainax is the credited studio, but the show was a joint venture from the start: it was produced under the "Project Eva." banner alongside Kadokawa Shoten, NAS, and TV Tokyo, with Tatsunoko Production a whole-series co-animation partner (also handling most of the photography). King Records ran music production for Sagisu's score. Buried in the per-episode breakdown, a few now-famous studios turn up doing uncredited contract work on individual episodes — Kyoto Animation on backgrounds for episodes 5 and 9, and SHAFT on cel painting for episodes 8-9 — alongside Studio Ghibli's episode 11.

links.label: The most famous of these one-off contract jobs
Why so much work ended up farmed out

entries.title: rec.arts.anime's first read on Asuka: "a total and complete brat"
entries.body: At least one rec.arts.anime poster's immediate reaction to Asuka's introduction was hostile, calling her a "total and complete brat" — one of several running threads on the newsgroup through the early episodes, alongside fans debating anime-technology details like the cushioning jets on NERV's power plugs and whether episode 10's magnetic Angel-trap would actually work.

links.label: How fast Japanese fandom caught up around the same time

entries.title: Comiket sold out on Eva before most fans had even seen the back half
entries.body: By Comiket 49 (December 29-30, 1995, its last year at the Arumi Fairgrounds), doujinshi circles were already flooding the show with fan content, despite having listed Gundam Wing on their booth applications months earlier — those were due the previous August, before Eva had even premiered. Soundtrack CDs and the first laser disc volume reportedly sold out in Japan around the same time, and the show revived a struggling garage-kit industry, mostly through figures of Asuka and Rei rather than the Eva units themselves.

links.label: The North American licensing news a couple months later

entries.title: Fans guessed the Rei/Yui connection mid-run — and got plenty else wrong
entries.body: Around episode 15, rec.arts.anime posters were already piecing together that the Evas had minds of their own and connecting Rei to Shinji's mother Yui, and drawing comparisons to science fiction writers Cordwainer Smith and Greg Bear. Other theories didn't survive contact with later episodes, notably a popular guess that Toji (piloting Unit-03) and Asuka would go on to work as a two-Eva team.

links.label: What the show actually revealed around this point

entries.title: "No longer a kids show": rec.arts.anime reacts to Bardiel
entries.body: One RAA regular who translated scripts for the fan community called this episode "very, very atrocious. Very cruel" and refused to translate it further; another poster accused him of running away from the story the same way its characters do, and a post relaying Japanese RAA sentiment reported calls for the show to be pulled off the air entirely. Because fans were staggered across the tape-trading pipeline at wildly different points, one person following along asked what had even happened — he'd only seen up through episode 3.

links.label: The episode fans were reacting to

entries.title: rec.arts.anime's read on the Misato/Kaji scene
entries.body: Western fans picked up the same controversy playing out in Japan: one RAA poster relayed that Japanese viewers were arguing the show shouldn't be airing an implied sex scene in an early-evening timeslot at all, and should have held it for a late-night broadcast instead.

links.label: The scene, and the Japanese broadcast controversy it caused

entries.title: ADV's license, announced mid-broadcast
entries.body: A.D. Vision — already negotiating with MOVIC, which held Eva's international distribution rights — announced on February 12, 1996 that it had won North American rights, surprising competitors who thought they had an inside track. Per co-founder and dub producer Matt Greenfield, MOVIC essentially told ADV the deal was happening rather than shopping it around. Fans were startled ADV landed it at all, given the company's reputation at the time for loose translations and fanservice/hentai releases through its SoftCel Pictures label.

links.label: The confusion ADV's own announcement immediately caused

entries.title: "OVA version"? ADV's own announcement confused everyone
entries.body: ADV's initial press release promised Eva "in a newly created OVA version ... with all new high-quality animation," setting off fan speculation that ranged from a Nautilus Story-style re-edit to a deliberately sanitized dub, with some Japanese fans guessing ADV had pressured Gainax to add sex and violence specifically for the American market. ADV's "Internet Liaison" David Williams clarified the next day that it just meant the full TV series re-rendered at OVA-level animation quality — which puzzled fans further, since the earliest episodes were already close to that standard.

links.label: The bigger controversy this announcement touched off

entries.title: "EvaGate '96"
entries.body: Four days after ADV's announcement, Gainax in-house translator Michael House posted a statement from GM Yasuhiro Takeda denying ADV held any rights and threatening legal action for copyright infringement; ADV's David Williams apologized for the confusion, saying MOVIC had told them the OVA-quality redo was already happening. RAA user Angst-sensei dubbed the standoff "EvaGate '96," announcing it like a prizefight: "There's the bell. It's time for round one of 'What the Hell is Going On?'" Most fansub groups still translating the show stopped once ADV's license was announced — per fansubber William Chow, unofficial subs were understood to have a "shelf life" that ended where an official release picked up.

links.label: How the standoff was eventually resolved

entries.title: The elevator scene, and giggling clones — as fans saw it at the time
entries.body: Contemporary reactions were more muted than the episode's later reputation suggests, but pointed: one Japanese-fan post relayed on RAA thought the Asuka/Rei elevator scene — since regarded as one of the show's most iconic moments — ran too long, and another found the Rei clones giggling during Naoko's reveal simply frightening rather than thematically loaded.

links.label: The scene, and its later critical reading

entries.title: The episode almost nobody posted about
entries.body: Unlike the outcry around episodes 18-20, rec.arts.anime barely discussed episode 24 at all. The closest thing to a documented contemporary reaction comes from Carl Horn's own account of watching it fansubbed: his impression of the minute-long shot of Unit-01's hand swung from suspicion of corner-cutting ("I bet the storyboards for this didn't take too long to draw") to admiration once it landed — "as usual, Anno's got a lot of guts."

links.label: How much louder that silence got two episodes later

entries.title: How angry fans actually got, in their own words
entries.body: Protoculture Addicts writers Claude J. Pelletier and Miyoko Graham collected Japanese fan reactions to the finale ranging from "I was stunned! I thought the ending was a bad joke!" to "I almost threw up!" and "I won't watch this show any longer!" On RAA, Western fans reached for comparisons like Mamoru Oshii's Urusei Yatsura 2: Beautiful Dreamer and the British series The Prisoner, or measured the ending against Gainax's own earlier Gunbuster.

links.label: The production explanations for why the finale turned out this way

entries.title: William Chow's theory for why the ending broke people
entries.body: Fansubber William Chow argues the finale violated an unwritten structural contract 26-episode shows of the era followed — a midpoint recap around episode 13, a crux around 24, resolution by 26 — and that Eva's refusal to resolve cleanly, paired with an ending left deliberately open, is what sent fans scrambling to fill the gap with their own theories about what "really" happened.

links.label: Staff accounts of why the finale took the shape it did

entries.title: Spike Spencer's on-mic reaction became an ADV home-video Easter egg
entries.body: ADV's English dub actor for Shinji, Spike Spencer, had no idea how the show ended going into the recording session. Producer Matt Greenfield let him rant on open mic once he found out, then played the recording back for every other cast member as they arrived — each of whom reacted the same way. The rant was later included as an Easter egg across ADV's home video releases of the series.

links.label: Eva's first major North American convention showing, a couple months later

entries.title: Third Impact staged as a therapy session
entries.body: One reading frames the whole Instrumentality sequence as a symbolic psychoanalytic process, with Rei guiding Shinji through his memories and traumas as an analyst would a patient — opening by pressing him to retract his claim that all of humanity should die. The Misato's-apartment setting the sequence begins in is read not as a physical memory but as a staging of Shinji's subconscious itself, where Asuka's refusal to help him draws out his defining line: "Don't leave me alone! Don't abandon me! Please don't kill me!"

links.label: The relational pattern this session is meant to break

entries.title: Rei's silence as a deliberate act, not an absence of one
entries.body: When child Shinji asks Rei "is it alright for me to be here?", her refusal to answer can be read as intentional rather than withholding: Shinji's core neurosis is his need for external validation to justify his own existence, so an analyst-figure affirming him would only reinforce it. Tearing that down first is what the film's own tagline gestures at — "the fate of destruction is also the joy of rebirth" — with Shinji visually rendered as scratched apart in the frames that follow.

links.label: The larger scene this moment belongs to

entries.title: A Freudian castration-anxiety reading of Shinji and Gendo
entries.body: Shinji's compulsive need for others' approval has been linked to Freudian castration anxiety: just as the theory holds that a boy fears his father will take his phallus as punishment, Shinji carries an unspoken fear that if he stops being useful, Gendo — who he holds responsible for losing Yui — will "kill" him too, even though nothing in the story states this literally.

links.label: How the show keeps Gendo deliberately unreadable to Shinji

entries.title: Oedipal undertones in Third Impact's staging
entries.body: A shot late in the sequence frames Shinji looking up first at Misato, then at Rei, in a composition read as deliberately sexually intimate — Misato as a surrogate mother who took him into her home, Rei as an (unbeknownst-to-Shinji) clone of Yui. Piloting Unit-01, which houses Yui's own soul, becomes literally Oedipal on this reading; because Yui died when Shinji was four, before his phallic-stage development had resolved on its own, his Oedipus complex never got the chance to subside the way Freudian theory says it normally would, leaving its influence running under his character for the rest of the story.

links.label: What Rei actually is, underneath the reading

entries.title: The LCL Sea as Lacan's Imaginary register
entries.body: Rei's description of Instrumentality — "an ambiguous world where it is impossible to tell where you end and other people begin" — maps onto Jacques Lacan's Imaginary register, the pre-language state before an infant distinguishes its own fragmented self from others. On this reading, the collapse of every individual's AT Field into a shared sea of LCL is Instrumentality literalizing that undifferentiated state at a species-wide scale.

links.label: How Shinji is read as leaving this state again

entries.title: Shinji's rejection of Instrumentality as Lacan's Mirror Stage
entries.body: Where Instrumentality is read as Lacan's Imaginary register, Shinji's exit from it has been read as Lacan's Mirror Stage: he recognizes his own reflection within the LCL sea and, in that act of self-recognition, separates himself back out from the collective unconscious — the same mechanism Lacan describes as giving rise to the ego. The End of Evangelion's soundtrack track "Interference of Others" is noted as an on-the-nose nod to the same idea, and the finale's own title pun ("the beast that shouted 'I' at the heart of the world") lands the same beat in miniature.

links.label: The state Shinji is separating himself out from
The broader TV-finale/EoE framing this choice echoes

entries.title: NERV read as a UN peace-enforcement operation
entries.body: International-law scholar Santiago Vargas Niño has analyzed NERV's mandate through the real UN Security Council framework for "peace enforcement operations" under Chapter VII of the UN Charter — the same legal basis behind, e.g., the 2013 Intervention Brigade authorized in the Democratic Republic of the Congo to proactively use force against non-state armed groups. On this reading, NERV's mandate to destroy the Angels fits that model closely enough that, as a UN subsidiary organ, it would arguably be bound by Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions and international humanitarian law more broadly.

links.label: What NERV actually is

entries.title: Unit-01's unpowered rampage as a lethal-autonomous-weapons case study
entries.body: Legal scholarship on lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS) has used Unit-01's uncommanded reactivation and kill of Sachiel as an illustrative worst case: a weapon acting on its own initiative, unpredictably, beyond its operators' control. The essay frames this against the real "techno-pessimist" vs. "techno-optimist" debate over whether such systems could ever reliably apply international humanitarian law's rules on distinguishing combatants from civilians and weighing proportionality — arguing the evidence needed to settle that question can only come from deploying the weapons in the first place, which is itself the problem.

links.label: The scene being read this way

entries.title: Why Toji's sister likely had no legal recourse against NERV
entries.body: Extending the UN-peace-enforcement reading, Vargas Niño argues NERV would inherit the UN's own broad immunity from domestic courts under the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the UN and the model Status of Forces Agreement — the same immunity real courts in the Netherlands, the United States, and the European Court of Human Rights have upheld for the UN itself. On that basis, a civilian hurt as collateral damage during an authorized operation like the Sachiel battle would have essentially no path to compensation, since her injury would likely be deemed proportionate to the operational necessity of stopping an extinction-level threat.

links.label: The civilian casualty this reading is built around

entries.title: Reading NERV's Earth as one giant psychoanalytic clinic
entries.body: One extended reading, drawing on Deleuze and Guattari's concept of the assemblage, frames the entire world of Evangelion as a planetary analytic clinic: its traumatized characters (Shinji, Rei, Asuka, Gendo, Ritsuko, Misato) are the analysands, while the Angels function as "Lesser Analysts" — brief, low-impact encounters that provoke expressions of repressed desire without resolving anything on their own. Two recurring figures, Kaji and later Kaworu, are cast as "Greater Analysts" instead, running longer sessions that actually move characters toward psychological resolution.

links.label: The first "Greater Analyst," and his sessions
The second "Greater Analyst"

entries.title: The GeoFront's three layers as a map of the psyche
entries.body: The same reading extends NERV's own underground architecture into a Lacanian topology: the GeoFront's visible surface stands in for the ego or persona, Central Dogma (housing the MAGI) for the Symbolic Order where signifiers circulate, and Terminal Dogma — the crucified Lilith, the LCL lake, the Eva graveyard, Rei's birthplace — for the unsignifiable Real: drives, jouissance, and the raw facts of life and death.

links.label: What's actually built into these layers

entries.title: Kaji as the story's first "Greater Analyst"
entries.body: Unlike the Angels' brief provocations, Kaji is read as running full analytic sessions: with Misato on the drunken car ride home this episode, drawing out her confession about her father, and later with Shinji across episodes 18 and 19. In the episode 19 watermelon-patch scene in particular, Kaji is read as doing something none of Shinji's other pressuring adults do — presenting piloting as a latent potential Shinji can choose to actualize rather than a demand disguised as a choice, which is why that decision reads as more genuinely his own.

links.label: The session with Misato this reading is built on
The choice this reading says Kaji made possible

entries.title: Kaworu as the story's second "Greater Analyst"
entries.body: On the same reading, Kaworu completes the analytic work Kaji began: letting Shinji kill him functions as one last session, surfacing Shinji's buried need for connection right before his lowest point. The reading also leans on his name, Tabris — said to mean "the Revealed" and to mark him as patron of free will — to tie together his double role as both the final Angel and, as Adam's soul in a Lilin body, effectively the first.

links.label: What that final session is read as revealing
The unresolved question of what Kaworu actually is

entries.title: Arael's light, read through Eastern Orthodox theology
entries.body: Eastern Orthodox theology holds that Heaven and Hell aren't separate places but different reactions of the soul to the same Uncreated Light of God — bliss for those in communion with it, torment for those who reject it. One reading maps this directly onto Arael's attack: the same light is neither cruel nor kind on its own, but forces Asuka's own repressed trauma to the surface, and it's what she's unwilling to face, not the light itself, that makes the experience torturous for her.

links.label: The attack this reading reinterprets

entries.title: A meta-critique: Eva as the object of its own diagnosis
entries.body: One closing argument holds that Evangelion, while structured to guide its audience toward the same kind of self-analysis its characters undergo, has for some fans become the neurotic symptom rather than the cure — pointing to the intensity of fan idolization around Rei specifically as an example. On this reading, Rei fulfills the Mother and Daughter archetypes but never the Lover, leaving her an "empty signifier" that an invested fandom fills with its own fantasy rather than engaging with as written.

links.label: The character this critique is aimed at

entries.title: Shinji and Asuka run the same arc, offset by a few episodes
entries.body: A close-reading fan theory lines up Shinji and Asuka's final-act beats as the same sequence, with Asuka consistently hitting each one first: an attempted-suicide moment (Asuka in 24, Shinji in 25), anger at the other for "not being there" for them (Asuka during Arael's attack in 22, Shinji across the hospital, kitchen, and hell-train scenes in 26), a reconciliation with their mother (Asuka in 25, Shinji in 26), a "breaking scream" (Asuka's flashing-kanji breakdown in 22 versus Shinji's silence after asking Rei "is it alright for me to be here?" in 26), a slide into detachment bordering on catatonia, and finally being used as a vessel by the Mass Production Evangelions (Asuka in 25, Shinji in 26). The theory argues this offset is why Asuka, having processed her own trauma slightly ahead of Shinji, is the one able to touch his cheek instead of rejecting him at the very end of The End of Evangelion.

links.label: Asuka's version of the "breaking scream" beat
Shinji's version of the same beat
Where this parallel is argued to pay off

entries.title: A fan theory: the Director's Cuts and EoE form a separate continuity from the On-Air finale
entries.body: One fan theory argues the show effectively splits into two internally consistent continuities from episode 22 or 23 onward: episodes 1-26 as originally broadcast, versus episodes 1-21 followed by the Director's Cut versions of 22-24 and then The End of Evangelion instead of the On-Air 25-26. It points to concrete differences between the On-Air and Director's Cut versions of the Armisael/Rei sequence, a redesigned Terminal Dogma and Eva graveyard, and roughly double the Rei clones visible in the Director's Cut tank — and further reads the apostrophe on the alternate episode titles as a deliberate nod to the mathematical/musical use of a prime mark to denote a transformed variant of the original, a reading voice actress Kotono Mitsuishi has jokingly gestured at regarding the Rebuild films' own use of the same mark. Streaming versions that splice the Director's Cuts of 22-24 into the On-Air 25-26, as Netflix does, merge what this theory treats as two separate branches into one.

links.label: The more conventional framing of how the TV finale and EoE relate
A related theory about impacts recurring across tellings
The sequence cited as the clearest On-Air/DC divergence

entries.title: Episode 26's abstract sequence read as Hegel's argument staged in dialogue
entries.body: The same reading walks through the TV finale's white-void sequence line by line as a near-literal staging of Hegel's argument: Shinji alone in "a world of nothing," told this is "perfect freedom," unable to act without anything to act on; other characters' voices handing him constraints one at a time — a floor, gravity, the ability to walk — as something like a will to perceive takes hold; and finally, once he has objects to relate to, the explicit lines "without others to interact with you cannot truly recognize your own image" and "by recognizing the differences between yourself and others, you establish your identity as yourself." The reading treats those lines as close to a direct paraphrase of Hegel's claim that self-consciousness exists only by being recognized by another self-consciousness, not merely by being distinct from objects.

links.label: A more conventional framing of how this sequence relates to EoE
How this dialogue is read as connecting to the strangling scene

entries.title: Asuka's caress echoed as Shinji's "first other"
entries.body: Episode 26's dialogue states "the very first other person is your mother" — an infant's mother being the first consciousness it ever encounters as separate from itself. This reading notes EoE gives Asuka's cheek-caress the same gesture used elsewhere for Yui, casting Asuka symbolically as the "first other" Shinji meets on waking from Instrumentality, reinforcing the film's birth and rebirth imagery around his emergence from the LCL sea. The reading is explicit that this isn't meant literally — Shinji and Asuka's relationship is treated as sexual, not maternal — only that her affection is read as filling the same reassurance Yui's death left missing from his development.

links.label: The Yui connection this gesture is read as echoing

entries.title: Anno, on the TV finale, in his own words
entries.body: In a 1996 interview conducted during EoE's production — quoted on the forum from a compiled interview archive attributed to researcher gwern — Anno described the TV finale as "a regression back into the self... I intended to push forward but ended up being drawn into this feeling of blockage." Asked directly whether the ending should be read as happy, he said: "there are probably people who see it as a happy ending. For me, personally, it wasn't very happy. In hindsight."

links.label: Other staff accounts of how the finale came together
Anno's much more defiant public defense of the same ending

entries.title: Whether EoE quietly repudiates the TV finale's ending
entries.body: Some posters argue EoE marks a real shift away from EoTV's message rather than just a variant retelling — pointing to concrete divergences (Misato's and Ritsuko's deaths differ between the two versions, as does the Misato/Kaji scene) and describing EoTV's ending as "triumphant" against EoE's "miserable and depressing" one, backed by Anno's own hindsight comments about the TV ending. Others push back that a vague, self-reflective interview shouldn't be read as a clear statement of authorial intent on its own — and the Hegel thread's own author acknowledged a real gap in his case: the choking scene at the center of the whole discussion has no equivalent moment anywhere in the TV finale.

links.label: The interview comments this argument leans on
A reading that treats the two endings as complementary rather than opposed

entries.title: A show working on four levels at once
entries.body: Critic Mike Crandol argues most allegorical fiction operates on two levels — the story itself and its symbolic meaning — but Evangelion runs on four simultaneously: a straightforward sci-fi action-adventure, a bleak satire of the giant-robot genre it belongs to, a coming-of-age parable, and a treatise on confronting loneliness and uncertainty as an adult. On this reading, the early episodes' deceptively conventional feel is doing real work — letting the other three layers build underneath a show that still reads, on its surface, like just another entry in an overcrowded genre.

entries.title: Episode 26's animation collapse, compared to "Duck Amuck"
entries.body: As the TV finale strips away plot for direct psychological interrogation, its visuals regress in step — full animation gives way to storyboards, which give way to a black-and-white scribble of Shinji adrift in a white void. Critic Mike Crandol compares the effect to the classic Chuck Jones Looney Tunes short "Duck Amuck," in which Daffy Duck's cartoon universe is dismantled around him by an unseen animator — reading Shinji's restrictions being handed to him one at a time (a line to stand on, "a top and a bottom," the ability to walk) as the show applying the same device to a psychological rather than comedic end.

links.label: A reading of the same sequence's dialogue

entries.title: How Cartoon Network censored episode 1 for broadcast
entries.body: When "Angel Attack" aired on Cartoon Network's Giant Robot Week block in February 2003, edits included cutting the opening animation entirely, softening dialogue to remove profanity (both Misato's and a general's "Damn!"), digitally erasing a joke note on Misato's photo directing Shinji's attention to her breasts, and cutting a shot of Shinji's hand covered in Rei's blood. Other material made it through untouched, including a full ashtray of cigarette butts, the show's cross-shaped explosions, and Misato telling Shinji "don't get killed out there" — and the airing wasn't the uncut, commercial-free broadcast some viewers had been led to expect.

entries.title: Cartoon Network's much heavier edit of episode 2
entries.body: "Unfamiliar Ceiling" got a far more aggressive cut for its 2003 Cartoon Network airing than the premiere, driven almost entirely by Misato's drinking and undress: her Yebisu beer cans were digitally recolored blue throughout, whole scenes built around her apartment's clutter of empty cans and liquor bottles were removed (including Shinji taking inventory of her second refrigerator and their Pen Pen conversation), her drying lingerie and a shot of a nude Shinji looking at it were cut, and a bath scene had her redrawn into a digital bikini. The Eva-vs-Sachiel violence fared no better — shots of Unit-01's blood-spraying head and of it breaking the Angel's arms and tearing open its chest were all cut, along with Ritsuko's "Berserker" line — though, as in episode 1, the cross-shaped explosions were left alone.

links.label: The same broadcast's edits to episode 1

entries.title: How to actually pronounce "Evangelion"
entries.body: A 2003-2004 back-and-forth in Anime News Network's Answerman column landed on a hard-G pronunciation, "Evan-GHEL-ion," matching the English dub, despite reader pushback arguing for a soft-G "Evan-JELL-yon" to match the word's Greek root Ευαγγέλιον ("gospel"/"good news"). The hard-G case won out: ancient Greek gamma is itself a hard G, the word's Japanese katakana rendering エヴァンゲリオン uses the hard-G ゲ rather than the soft-G ジェ despite Japanese having a perfectly usable je sound (the cast's ability to pronounce it correctly elsewhere, e.g. Cowboy Bebop's "Jet Black," ruled out simple mispronunciation), and the specific "v" spelling (versus the Greek upsilon) traces to the word's Latin form, Evangelium, rather than the Greek original.

entries.title: A harsh 1998 review of the flashback-heavy narration in episodes 21-24
entries.body: One of the earliest published English-language reviews of the finale, by Kenneth Lee for Anime News Network, singled out episode 21's rapid-fire flashback structure for criticism: the narration jumps between Fuyutsuki's own memories, an apparently impossible first-person account of Naoko murdering the first Rei, present-day Misato listening to a tape, and Kaji's own recorded words, all within a few minutes. The review argued this "MTV-style" barrage of information looks like it's answering the show's biggest outstanding questions — how Yui died, who Rei is, why Kaji died — while actually leaving most of them unresolved.

entries.title: A contemporary complaint about the music playing over Asuka's suffering
entries.body: The same 1998 review singled out the choral, celebratory religious music playing during Arael's psychic assault on Asuka — which the reviewer names as "Symphony No. 9 in D-minor, the 'Alleluia' song" — as one of the worst music cues in the show, arguing it reads as incongruous whichever way it's meant: as sincere accompaniment to Asuka's breakdown, or as expressing the Angel's own perspective.

links.label: The scene this music plays over

entries.title: Rei II's arc as a compressed "puppet becomes human" story
entries.body: Critic Kenneth Lee compares Rei II's rapid development of what looks like a soul — learning gratitude when she thanks Shinji for cleaning her room, learning to smile, being told by Toji that she has a purpose, and finally choosing to sacrifice herself to protect Shinji — to the familiar "puppet becomes human" arc of Pinocchio or Key the Metal Idol. His complaint isn't that the parallel doesn't work, but that a premise substantial enough to carry an entire series on its own gets compressed into a handful of episodes before Rei dies.

links.label: The death this arc builds toward

entries.title: A criticized one-line dismissal of Toji, Kensuke, and Hikari
entries.body: After building up Toji as a sympathetic tragic figure across several episodes — his growing friendship with Shinji, his relationship with Hikari, and his crippling injury as Unit-03's pilot — the show writes all three off with a single line of Shinji's narration: "The city was destroyed, so they had to move away." Kenneth Lee's 1998 review holds this up as the clearest example of the finale discarding secondary characters the moment their plot usefulness runs out, with none of the three getting so much as a farewell scene.

links.label: The injury this writeoff follows

entries.title: A "sins of the fathers" reading across four generations
entries.body: Kenneth Lee's 1998 review proposes a shared pattern across the show's main parent/child pairs, modeled on the Exodus line about the sins of the parents being visited on their children: Naoko's affair and betrayal echoed in Ritsuko's own entanglement with Gendo; Misato's father dying in pursuit of the truth behind Second Impact echoed in Misato's own reckless disregard for her safety chasing the same secrets; Kyoko's breakdown and suicide after Angel contact echoed in Asuka's breakdown and suicide attempt after her own; and Gendo's willingness to die for his convictions echoed in Shinji's repeated willingness to risk death for his. The review treats the pattern as suggestive rather than something the text confirms outright.

links.label: The first half of the Naoko/Ritsuko pairing
The first half of the Kyoko/Asuka pairing

entries.title: Early, skeptical criticism of the pace of Shinji and Kaworu's bond
entries.body: Alongside far more sympathetic later readings, Kenneth Lee's 1998 review is an early example of criticism aimed squarely at how quickly Shinji and Kaworu's relationship is drawn — arguing it's implausible for a character established across twenty episodes as guarded and withdrawn. The review specifically contrasts Shinji recoiling from Misato's comforting touch right after Rei's death with his acceptance of Kaworu's touch soon after meeting him, reading the shift as unearned rather than as a deliberate contrast.

links.label: A more sympathetic reading of the same relationship

entries.title: An early, harshly negative published review of the finale
entries.body: Kenneth Lee's September 1998 Anime News Network editorial is one of the earliest published English-language reviews of the finale, and among its harshest: it argues episodes 21-26 abandon the narrative foundation built across the first twenty episodes, dismisses the introspective closing episodes as failed "art-house" pretension rather than earned catharsis, and singles out Kaworu's line "death is the only true freedom" as especially ironic — coming, as the review points out, from a character who is himself an Angel.

links.label: Production-side explanations for how the finale took shape

entries.title: Anno's own explanation of the title, to a class of schoolkids
entries.body: In a 1999 NHK special where Anno returned to his old elementary school to teach a class, a student asked why the show was called Evangelion. Anno's answer: "It comes from a Christian word meaning 'Gospel,' and it's supposed to bring blessings. It has some Greek roots. I chose the name because it sounds complicated."

links.label: The etymology this explanation touches on

entries.title: Anno's hometown, and how much of it ended up on screen
entries.body: The same 1999 special returns Anno to Ube, his hometown in Yamaguchi Prefecture — a struggling factory town dominated by smog, smokestacks, and power lines, built around a chemical plant. The reviewer covering the special notes how directly Eva's own visual signature (power lines strung across man-made landscapes, industrial infrastructure) traces back to these surroundings, going so far as to say the imagery makes you expect to see Asuka round the corner.

entries.title: Anno, asked directly about self-esteem, in 1999
entries.body: Fielding questions from his old schoolkids, Anno was open about his own self-regard: "I'm not crazy about myself. I'm often told that those who don't like themselves have high ideals, but I think someone who says that doesn't really understand the pain that's involved." Asked which parts of his own anime he dislikes, he answered: "The parts that I'm in."

links.label: How this self-regard is read into the finale itself
The backlash Anno faced around the same period

entries.title: A few details about young Anno
entries.body: Interviewed by the schoolkids for the same special, Anno's parents and childhood friends filled in a few details: he was rejected from a childhood painting contest and turned his attention to manga afterward, loved watching the stars, and wrote his elementary-school graduation essay about his frustration at not being allowed to draw manga in class. He also recalled attending a Gundam exhibition on a department store rooftop as a kid.

entries.title: A show in two structural halves: obsession, then atmosphere
entries.body: Critic Tim Henderson divides the series into two halves that work in different registers: the first breeds obsession through brisk, accessible, almost Hollywood-textbook screenwriting that balances comedy, action, and drama, while the second breathes atmosphere instead, working on the viewer through the fabric of how episodes are put together rather than through fresh intellectual puzzle-solving. On this reading, the first half's very familiarity and comfort is what allows the second half's departure from it to land as hard as it does.

entries.title: A show that satisfies classical narrative theory, then detonates it
entries.body: Henderson frames Eva's structure against David Bordwell and Kristin Thompson's account of what audiences expect from narrative film: connected incidents building toward some resolved or newly-illuminated conflict. For most of its run Eva plays directly into this — the Jet Alone episode is cited as the clearest early evidence that NERV has an agenda beyond the Angels, and the opening credits themselves flash forward to a younger Misato, Kaji, and Ritsuko together, plus a glimpse of Kaworu, proof the endgame was mapped out from the start. By the final two episodes, though, this reading holds that the show detonates the very framework it spent twenty-plus episodes satisfying, pushing forward in a way classical narrative theory simply can't account for — dragging the audience's own built-up expectations along with it, which Henderson treats as a root cause of the backlash against the ending.

links.label: The episode cited as early evidence of a bigger agenda
Production-side explanations for the same rupture

entries.title: Shinji's Walkman as a Deleuzian "face"
entries.body: Henderson reads Shinji's ever-present cassette Walkman through a Deleuzian theory of cinematic affect, in which expression comes from micro-movement on an otherwise still, "reflective" surface — the same principle that makes a clock face or a gleaming knife blade feel expressive. The Walkman is mostly shown reaching the end of a tape side and flipping, until one scene in episode 9 breaks the pattern: as Asuka sleepwalks over and presses herself toward him, Shinji's startled finger slips and sends the tape into fast-forward, transmitting a jolt of urgency straight to the audience without a line of dialogue.

entries.title: Anno's own defense of the TV finale, in print
entries.body: Responding to the backlash in Protoculture Addicts issue #43, Anno stood by the original ending without qualification: "Most anime fans are furious. I understand their anger. I can't help laughing when hard-core anime fans say that we did a very lousy job, with intentional negligence. No we didn't. No staff members did a lousy job. In fact, every member at Gainax gave more energy than anybody can imagine. I feel sad that those fans couldn't see our efforts. Personally I think the original TV ending we showed ended up beautifully."

links.label: The fan reactions this is responding to
One theory for why the ending provoked this reaction at all
Anno's much more private doubts about the same ending

entries.title: EoE's two halves had two different directors
entries.body: "Air/Love is Destructive" — built around the roughly 27 minutes of new footage first previewed in Death & Rebirth — was helmed by Kazuya Tsurumaki, who has gone on to work on every Evangelion theatrical release since. "Sincerely Yours/ONE MORE FINAL: I need you," the film's second half, was directed by Anno himself.

links.label: Where each half's title actually comes from
The earlier film this footage first appeared in

entries.title: The plot is a vehicle, not the point
entries.body: Henderson argues Eva's actual plot, taken on its own terms, is "quite silly" — a jellyfish-shaped Angel threatening to replace humanity as the dominant species, a diamond-bodied Angel with a drill for a body, an orange "teething ring" shape that flies — but that this doesn't make the show badly written, since "good writing" and "good stories" aren't the same thing. On this reading, the monster-of-the-week format and its gimmicky Angel premises are a scaffold carrying the show's real content (character expression) rather than being that content themselves — pointing to how a diamond-drill Angel becomes the occasion for an ambitious countrywide sniping operation, or a flying "teething ring" becomes a tense race-against-time game of catch.

entries.title: Anno, on why the ending is left so open
entries.body: Asked by Newtype magazine about the ambiguity running through Evangelion's ending, Anno said: "we're offering viewers to think by themselves, so that each person can imagine his/her own world."

links.label: Other staff accounts of how the finale came together

entries.title: A formalist reading: visual echoes as scene-linking devices, not hidden meaning
