entries.body: Forum poster Eva Yojimbo raises a more skeptical, formalist question about Evangelion's habit of visually rhyming distant scenes — most notably, Shinji's tears falling on Asuka's cheek recurring in both the opening credits and the "One More Final" closing scene. He compares this to a technique common in older multi-storyline films, citing Kenji Mizoguchi's Ugetsu, where visually similar shots (there, two different characters each killing someone in a near-identical manner) link otherwise unrelated storylines without necessarily implying a deeper causal or thematic connection. On this reading, some of Eva's much-parsed visual callbacks might function primarily as formal nods to earlier moments rather than encoded clues to Asuka's state of mind or the "true" meaning of her final line.

links.label: The scene this skepticism is aimed at

entries.title: A political reading of "Congratulations": Japan as a nation of children
entries.body: Forum poster Eva Yojimbo connects the TV finale's closing line, "To all the children — congratulations," to Anno's stated feeling that postwar Japan was a nation of children trying to grow up too fast to catch up with the West. On this reading, the line isn't only about Shinji's personal psychological growth — it's also a political and generational statement about Japan's own compressed, pressured modernization.

links.label: The more personal reading of this same finale

entries.title: A divide in reception: political work in Japan, psychological work in the West
entries.body: Forum poster Eva Yojimbo argues that Japanese audiences and critics have tended to receive Evangelion as a fundamentally political work engaging with modern Japanese identity, duty, and the costs of the country's rapid postwar advancement, while Western fandom has more often read it as an existential, psychological character study — a gap he attributes partly to how few Japanese voices participate directly in English-language Eva discussion.

entries.title: A meta reading: the final line as Anno addressing disappointed fans
entries.body: Forum poster Razeil100 suggests Asuka's closing "kimochi warui" isn't really a line spoken by Asuka as a character at all, but one spoken through her — Anno's own message to fans who had reacted badly to the TV finale, a pointed response to being pushed to revisit and "bastardize" his original vision with a second ending.

links.label: How the line was actually written and directed

entries.title: A color shift between the TV finale and EoE's ending
entries.body: Forum poster Eva Yojimbo notes a deliberate color shift between the TV series' "happy, surreal" finale and the harsh presentation of EoE's closing scene, even before anything happens in it — reading the blue-to-red shift as visually encoding the tonal gulf between the two endings, ahead of the strangling itself reinforcing that harshness as "reality" reasserting itself after Instrumentality.

links.label: A broader red/blue color-symbolism theory applied elsewhere on the page

entries.title: A few continuity questions fans have never fully resolved
entries.body: Among a list of open questions essayist Steve Gilham compiled after a first viewing: how Unit-00's and Unit-02's in-story activation dates (2014 and 2015) square with Yui and Kyoko supposedly undergoing their contact experiments around the same time in 2004; and, more pointedly, what Shinji actually means when he tells Misato "I've done terrible things to Asuka" if the earlier strangling attempt during Instrumentality was only ever a fantasy that never physically happened — a line that reads oddly if nothing had actually occurred between them.

entries.title: Asuka's armor as the Hedgehog's Dilemma from the other side
entries.body: Essayist Steve Gilham reads Asuka's loud, aggressive exterior as the same underlying problem Shinji has, expressed in the opposite direction: where Shinji withdraws to avoid being hurt, Asuka's prickliness is a defensive performance covering the same fear of rejection — both of them navigating the same Hedgehog's Dilemma from opposite poles. Given her background (barely a teenager, already fast-tracked through university, and marked by her mother's suicide before she turned four), he argues that managing even this much of an approximation to normal social behavior is impressive rather than a character flaw.

links.label: The parable this reading applies to Asuka specifically

entries.title: A Taming of the Shrew parallel for the closing scene
entries.body: Essayist Steve Gilham draws a comparison between EoE's final scene and Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew, specifically as staged in the feminist-polemic productions that read the play as gruelling rather than romantic — a tonal register he finds similar to EoE's ending. He notes this reading gets unexpected support from trivia: concept art for the unrealized live-action Evangelion film reportedly renamed Asuka "Kate Rose," after the Shrew's own Katherine.

links.label: The scene this comparison is drawn to

entries.title: The GeoFront's stated dimensions don't actually add up
entries.body: Working through the show's own stated figures — a sphere 13.75km across, 89% buried, with only a 900m-high, 6km-wide cap exposed — essayist Steve Gilham calculates that an 11%-exposed spherical cap and a cap of those specific dimensions are mathematically inconsistent with each other: the stated height and width actually correspond to roughly 1.2% of the sphere's volume being exposed, not 11%. However fictional the underlying physics, the GeoFront's own geometry doesn't check out against itself.

links.label: The organization the GeoFront serves as headquarters for

entries.title: Working out Giant Rei's impact energy, and what it implies about who comes back
entries.body: Essayist Steve Gilham runs the numbers on Giant Naked Rei's collapse into the Pacific at the end of EoE — roughly 100 miles tall, and (assuming a flesh-like density) calculated to release energy comparable to a dinosaur-extinction-scale asteroid impact. Taking that scale of devastation seriously, he reads the ending's ambiguous fate for humanity pessimistically: rather than everyone quietly resuming their old lives, most of post-Instrumentality humanity would have little reason to want to return to a ravaged Earth at all, remaining instead as disembodied consciousness in the red-tinted band visible in the sky (bled, in this reading, from Rei's neck wound) — with Shinji and Asuka as special, privileged exceptions forced back into physical bodies rather than granted the same choice.

links.label: The broader unresolved question this calculation is trying to answer
The transformation whose scale this calculation is based on

entries.title: Discarded alternate shots for EoE's closing beats
entries.body: Surviving pre-production art shows at least two discarded alternate beats for the ending: one in which Asuka scornfully kicks over Shinji's grave marker, rather than the version that shipped, which simply shows it already fallen; and one in which Shinji is shown holding hands with what turns out to be a disembodied arm. Some read the finished film's own shot of just Asuka's severed forearm as a surviving, darker echo of that scrapped beat.

links.label: The finished version of this ending

entries.title: Evidence that episode 25 and EoE unfold concurrently
entries.body: Scattered within the TV finale's largely abstract episode 25, before its "Congratulations" sequence, are brief inserted shots that only make sense if EoE's physical events are already unfolding at the same time: Unit-02 sitting in a lake, Asuka feeling useless at her controls, Ritsuko dissolved into LCL, and Misato's death. Cited as evidence that the TV finale and EoE aren't meant as two separate, mutually exclusive endings so much as two views onto the same underlying event.

links.label: The more general framing of how the two endings relate

entries.title: Third Impact read as a Technological Singularity "hard takeoff"
entries.body: Essayist Steve Gilham reads Third Impact through the lens of the Technological Singularity — the idea, from futurist Vernor Vinge, that recursive self-improvement could abruptly produce superhuman intelligence. On this reading, Giant Naked Rei — a fusion of Adam, Lilith, Rei, and fragments of Yui — is the suddenly emergent transhuman intelligence, while the many "lesser Reis" appearing to each character in the form of their most beloved person function like Singularitarian "Transition Guides," bridging ordinary humanity and whatever comes after it. Because Gendo occupies a privileged, unfriendly position at the controls rather than a neutral one, the reading treats Third Impact as an involuntary, non-benevolent version of what Singularitarian writing calls a "hard takeoff." Gilham traces the reading's textual hook back to episode 2's title card for the "Human Instrumentality Project ... Business Plan Outline," glimpsed well before Third Impact is ever explained.

links.label: The in-story program this reading builds on
The transformation read here as an emergent superintelligence

entries.title: The fandom Eva walked into, and how word of it first got out
entries.body:
Gainax already had an American fan base before Eva existed: its Daicon opening films had played at US conventions years earlier, Toren Smith had shared a house with studio staff, and fans met the crew at the 1987 Los Angeles premiere of Royal Space Force (then titled Star Quest) — the studio went on to co-present AnimeCon91, the convention that set the template for Anime Expo and Otakon (the latter named for Gainax's own Otaku no Video). That fan base had to make do with what tape trading could supply: in 1995, official anime in North America was scarce and expensive — early distributors like AnimEigo, US Renditions, and A.D. Vision had only just formed, and a single tape could run $45-50 — so raw or home-recorded episodes moved from Japanese video stores and Japan-based contacts to fansubbing groups like William Chow's Arctic Animation, who copied and mailed tapes to anyone who sent blank cassettes and return postage.

Japanese audiences first heard of the show itself through Gainax's own newsletter G.Press and the start of Sadamoto's manga adaptation in the February 1995 issue of Shōnen Ace (on sale December 1994) — but the earliest press coverage anywhere ran a beat earlier, in the American magazine Animerica that same February, beating Japanese anime magazines like Newtype and Animage to the story. Sourced from a conversation at a Gainax party the previous December, that scoop described alien "Disciples" who demand humanity halt its genetic-engineering research and grant a grace period before returning — language that didn't survive to broadcast but traces back to Gainax's late-1993 pitch documents and preliminary Sadamoto/Yamashita sketches later reprinted in the art book Der Mond. Animerica's June 1995 follow-up (drawing on Newtype's April coverage) quoted Anno dismissing the mecha genre as stale — "Don't you think that robot animation is behind the times? ... It's not a refreshing or new genre" — and speculated the show would land as a cult favorite rather than a mainstream hit on the scale of Nadia or Royal Space Force. About 200 fans got an even earlier look than that: episodes 1 and 2 previewed at the second Gainax Festival in Itako, Ibaraki, on July 22–23, 1995, showing only the raw episodes since the opening sequence and other finishing elements weren't ready yet. Its actual TV debut got an odd lead-in: on September 27, 1995, a week before the premiere, TV Tokyo aired the final episode of the 1987 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles series and followed it immediately, in the same slot, with a commercial for the new show.

links.label: How Western fans saw the show days before this broadcast even aired

entries.title: A fan-made VHS premiere, five days ahead of Japan's broadcast — and how newsgroup opinion reacted
entries.body:
Anime Weekend Atlanta organizer Gordon Waters got a raw tape and a rough translation from a Japanese graduate student, then spent the weekend of October 20-22, 1995 timing subtitles with friends Daric Koslowski and Matt Murray using JACOSUB — a fan-written subtitling program, one of the first of its kind, run on a Commodore Amiga with a video clock synchronizer. The finished fansub premiered October 27 to a packed room at AWA's Castlegate Hotel, five days before most Western fans could see the episode any other way; industry figures Jerry Chu (Bandai), Robert Woodhead (AnimEigo), and Neil Nadelman (U.S. Manga Corps) were in the crowd. It screened again weeks later at New Jersey's Anime East, alongside raw copies of episodes 2-4.

On the Usenet newsgroup rec.arts.anime, early posts favorably compared the episode to contemporary OVAs and praised Megumi Hayashibara's performance as Rei as a departure from the loud, brash roles she usually played, like Ranma from Ranma ½ — with some posters already speculating about the nature of the three pilots.

links.label: The newsgroup's reaction a few episodes later

entries.title: The original pitch: Raziel/Rajiel, a two-part opener, and a wildly different endgame
entries.body:
Gainax's original 1993 pitch document had this episode titled "People's Reunion" and structured as a diptych with episode 2. It was to open with Shinji stuck on a train during a battle between Rei's Eva-00 and a "metallic" Angel named Raziel (rendered elsewhere as "Rajiel"), who vanishes into a lake, sending a damaged Unit-00 back to base; the start of a separate fight between the Angel and a berserk Unit-01 was also planned for this episode before being pushed into episode 2.

A fuller pre-production episode outline (reproduced from the 100% Newtype Collection) shows just how different the whole series' original plan was from what aired: the endgame was built around a "Human Completion Program" rather than Instrumentality, a location called "Aluka" served as a "promised land," Eva units 05 and 06 were sent from Germany, and the 12th Angel erased the Americas outright. Read against the aired series, the outline shows both the shadows of episodes that did make it to screen and plot threads more radical than even most fan fiction attempts.

links.label: Another scrapped early-draft concept
Part of why the finished show drifted so far from this outline

quote.original: 当初の案では、列車に乗っていたシンジが、綾波レイの操縦するエヴァ零号機と使徒「ラジエル」の戦闘により足止めを食らう場面から始まる予定であった。その戦闘でラジエルは湖へと姿を消し、損傷した零号機はNERV本部へと帰還するという流れである。
quote.translation: "In the original plan, the episode was to open with Shinji stuck on a train during a battle between Rei Ayanami's piloted Eva Unit-00 and the Angel 'Raziel'; in that battle Raziel would vanish into a lake, and the damaged Unit-00 would return to NERV headquarters."

entries.title: Megazone 23: Anno's mentor, and a likely uncredited structural precursor
entries.body:
Before Evangelion, a twenty-something Anno worked as a freelance animator on the original 1985 Megazone 23 OAV for studio AIC, around the same period he was presenting short films at Daicon and impressing Hayao Miyazaki with his work on Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind. On Megazone 23, and earlier on Space Runaway Ideon and The Super Dimension Fortress Macross, Anno worked alongside animator Ichirō Itano — creator of the swarming-missile "Itano Circus" technique — whom he came to regard as a mentor. At the 2014 Tokyo International Film Festival, Anno credited his admiration for Itano's work on the Mobile Suit Gundam franchise as the reason he pursued a career in animation in the first place.

Critic Jonny Lobo argues the OAV itself deserves more recognition as a likely influence on Evangelion than it typically gets: a secret city built beneath an older Tokyo and shielded by massive moving mechanisms (echoing NERV's Geofront), biblical names used mostly for exotic flavor rather than deep symbolism, human-like extraterrestrial antagonists that provoke existential and epistemological crises rather than straightforward action, and technology cast as a mother figure to disoriented teenage leads. Lobo extends the parallel all the way to The End of Evangelion: both EoE and Megazone 23 Part II open on scenes of mass destruction scored to music that reads as melancholic and rapturous at once — "Komm, süsser Tod" in EoE's case, "Himitsu Kudasai" in Megazone 23's — a pairing he reads as more than coincidence, tying both works' suggestion that large-scale societal collapse is inevitable and cyclical to the wider Y2K-era anxieties (rapture fiction, millennial unease) both franchises were made and watched within.

entries.scene: The final shot, on the beach
entries.title: Eight competing readings of the strangling itself
entries.body:
One long-running reading (posted by user sephirotic) takes the strangling as Shinji's first genuinely active, aggressive act after a lifetime of passivity — a wordless "stop hurting me" from someone who likes Asuka and has never before been able to resist being pushed away, rather than a sign of hatred or a breakdown into violence. On this reading, his tears afterward aren't guilt at the act itself but shock: braced for the rejection he expects, he gets tenderness instead, and that's what breaks him.

Poster Sanada Yukimura pushed back on that "unafraid to connect" framing with a dog-behavior analogy: a dog that barks a lot but never bites can be less dangerous than a quiet one that lashes out only when it feels genuinely cornered, so lashing out isn't automatically evidence of openness — it can just as easily be self-defense. Their own alternative is bleaker: Shinji's attempt to kill Asuka is read as an act of mercy, meant to spare her from a post-Instrumentality world he no longer believes can offer real happiness — a much darker note than the TV finale, where Shinji explicitly comes to believe a good life is possible.

Poster Azathoth reads the strangling as deliberately paralleling the film's earlier masturbation scene: both are framed as Shinji acting purely on his own wounded feelings at Asuka's expense, rather than reckoning with why she pushed him away. On this reading the self-indulgence runs all the way up to triggering Instrumentality itself, making the strangling scene's ending a final test — Asuka reaches out anyway, and Shinji's response is to sob rather than accept it, which isn't the outcome she was hoping to get out of the gesture.

Forum poster FreakyFilmFan4ever reads the strangling as staged to mirror Unit-01's fight with Sachiel back in episode 2: in both, a body sits pinned atop another, and the pinned party reaches up toward the other's face — Sachiel to tear down Unit-01's AT Field, Asuka to caress Shinji's cheek. Poster Reichu offered a correction worth keeping alongside it: Sachiel's AT Field was actually neutralized earlier, when Unit-01 forced its core open, not by the embrace itself — and Eva-01 straddling something (Sachiel, Eva-03, Zeruel) is consistently a killing posture in the show, making Shinji's initial position a mirror of his Eva's murderous instinct, with the difference being that — unlike his mother inside it — he can actually be talked down.

Some fans read a deliberate pairing with the moment, flashed just afterward, of Naoko's silhouette strangling Rei I: both Rei I and Asuka verbally put distance between their strangler and Gendo in the moment (Rei I calling Naoko an "old hag," Asuka calling Shinji "Daddy's Boy"). On this reading, the difference is the outcome — Naoko couldn't let go of her toxic attachment to Gendo as her lover and the encounter ends in death, while Shinji can let go of his to Gendo as his father, and stops once he feels Asuka's touch.

Poster StrokeMeGoat points out that every other strangling in the show — including Shinji's own strangling of Asuka earlier, at the start of Instrumentality — shows both thumbs stacked together over the windpipe, the standard lethal grip. In the beach scene, though, Shinji's thumbs instead line up separately over each carotid artery, which would cut off blood flow and cause someone to pass out rather than asphyxiate; combined with how visibly he's trembling, the reading holds that Shinji may be testing whether Asuka is real and checking for a pulse rather than trying to kill her outright — something poster C.T.1290 separately described as "strangling her to confirm her existence."

Poster VoidEater reads the scene as capturing Shinji and Asuka mid-reintegration, briefly acting without the social "ego" self that normally filters them: Shinji finally lets out the anger and resentment he's built up over how Asuka has treated him, while Asuka finally shows the desire she's kept hidden. As their egos fully reassert themselves, Shinji catches himself and draws back.

Outside the forum, critic Mike Crandol draws a direct line between the TV series' lighthearted first kiss and this much darker counterpart: where Asuka's earlier kiss ends in her fleeing in mock disgust, one of Shinji's pre-Instrumentality head-trips restages the same beat with a confession of love instead of a kiss, and Asuka accuses him of loving her only as a convenient source of comfort. Unable to bear the accusation, Shinji strangles her within the vision itself, foreshadowing the real strangling later in the film — reframing that later scene as the culmination of an anxiety the show planted episodes earlier.

entries.scene: The final shot, on the beach
entries.title: Three more debates: the caress, and what "kimochi warui" actually means
entries.body:
Forum posters split over what Asuka's cheek-touch is actually doing. One camp (including a reading attributed to longtime poster Mr. Tines) takes it as gratitude — thanks for being willing to end her life. Others read it as her finally offering Shinji the gentleness he'd begged for and been refused earlier, on the hell train. A counter-argument (from poster Bagheera) pushes back on the gratitude reading specifically: if Asuka actually wanted to die, tenderness is close to the worst tool available, since Shinji is starved for affection and receiving it — rather than rejection — is what's shown to break him down, not drive him to finish the act.

Fans also disagree on how to read Asuka's closing line in context. Some argue it's consistent with her established character rather than a softening — pointing out her glare on the beach visually echoes her glare at Shinji during the earlier kitchen breakdown, and that showing him a moment of kindness doesn't obligate her to find his crying any less pathetic by her own standards. Others (including a reading from poster sephirotic) read it as something closer to regret or an apology for how she'd treated him, rather than renewed rejection. The scene's shooting script originally had Shinji respond by calling her "baka" (idiot) — a deliberate callback to the show's opening train-platform scene — before the line was cut for tone.

A third reading (summarized on the forum from a separate Hegel-influenced analysis) argues Shinji and Asuka don't fully snap back into themselves the instant they leave the LCL sea — the two lie beside each other silent and expressionless before visibly "waking up" through the exchange that follows, paralleling how the beach caress reverses the earlier rejection at the start of Instrumentality. On this reading, Asuka's final line specifically calls back to the hospital-room scene: inside Instrumentality, with no barriers between people, Asuka acknowledges what Shinji did there and even permits his attraction to her on her own terms; back in reality, with those barriers restored, she reacts to that same memory with disgust instead — making the line about that particular moment rather than a blanket judgment of him.

entries.title: A Hegelian "struggle for recognition" reading of the strangling — and how far its own author would push it
entries.body:
EoE's official recap card states Shinji chokes Asuka "to feel the existence of an 'other'. To confirm... rejection and denial." Forum poster zlink64 reads that line through the "Lordship and Bondage" section of Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit: two self-conscious beings must risk a struggle to the death for the other's recognition, but the one who wins must stop short of actually killing the other, or the recognition that was the whole point is lost along with them. On this reading, Shinji strangling Asuka and then stopping directly re-enacts that structure — he needs her continued, independent existence, not her death, to have his own reality confirmed by someone who could deny him.

zlink64 later extended the reading further: rather than one party staying fixed in the dominant role, the beach exchange has Shinji and Asuka trade positions — Shinji rejects (strangling) while Asuka accepts (the caress), then Asuka rejects in turn (her final line) while Shinji is left to accept it. Since Hegel's account has the subordinate party, not the dominant one, end up achieving full self-consciousness through the exchange, this reading treats the reciprocal swap as the healthiest version of the dynamic on offer. Fellow poster StrokeMeGoat added that Rei's ghostly appearance to Shinji just before the strangling, paired with Rei and Kaworu's earlier framing of themselves as "hope that people might one day understand one another," reads as foreshadowing this reconciliation rather than undercutting it.

Several posters pushed back on treating Hegel as a confirmed direct source, pointing out that Anno has said elsewhere he never read Kierkegaard — making close familiarity with Hegel's specific essay unlikely, with culturally-diffused ("osmosis") exposure to the idea a more plausible explanation. One reply proposed a more parsimonious lineage: Jacques Lacan, who absorbed Hegel's ideas via Alexandre Kojève's lectures (and Husserl via Sartre, and Freud via de Saussure and Heidegger), would be a more likely single point of contact if Anno studied psychoanalysis through Lacan rather than each of those thinkers individually. zlink64 eventually backed off the stronger claim, framing Hegel less as "confirmed inspiration" and more as simply the clearest available vocabulary for explaining the abstract idea of "the Other" to readers unfamiliar with it.

entries.title: Eva Yojimbo's red/blue duality theory: Asuka vs. Rei, fists vs. palms, and the beach as replay
entries.body:
An extended fan theory (posted by Eva Yojimbo) argues Anno consistently codes Asuka in red — tied to sexuality, harsh reality, and an individual life separated from others by their AT Field — against Rei in blue, tied to origins (Lilith and Yui), motherhood, Instrumentality, and the "collective unconscious." On this reading, Shinji's arc throughout the series and EoE alike is a choice between the two poles, summed up in a line the theory attributes to longtime poster Reichu: Shinji "leaves MOTHER for his SIGNIFICANT OTHER."

The same theory tracks a recurring gesture pairing across the series: closed fists consistently associated with death (including in Eva battles), open palms with life — citing the Gates of Guf located in Lilith's own palms, and the bookend shots of Shinji with blood on his hands over Rei versus semen on his hands over Asuka. Shinji's hands clenching and unclenching are read as tracking the show's recurring question of what choice and action actually look like for him, most directly voiced as "what are your hands for?"

It extends to the closing choke-then-caress exchange itself, read as deliberately re-staging the moment Instrumentality began: Shinji symbolically "chooses" death by strangling Asuka and everything she represents, and is answered inside Instrumentality by Yui's own caress as he re-emerges into reality — a link the theory ties to a red streak visible across the moon (itself coded blue/Rei/Lilith) at that moment. On the beach, Shinji is read as trying to "kill" the fresh pain of rebirth into individual, harsh reality by strangling Asuka again; releasing his grip is what actually accepting that reality looks like, while Asuka's caress reaffirms "we're alive" — offered as hope rather than any promise that things get easier.

entries.title: Gilham's five-stage Complementation framework, and his two competing readings of the ending
entries.body:
Essayist Steve Gilham proposes reading Complementation as unfolding in five distinct stages. "Coalescence" begins with Shinji and Asuka in intimate spiritual contact. "Expansion" folds in the recently deceased, including Misato's uncensored regrets about Shinji and her memories of Kaji. "Reiteration" twists earlier show moments into new shapes — the episode 15 kiss recurs as a kick, and Shinji's callous "Kaji is dead, Asuka" from episode 24 resurfaces — separated by a scene replaying Shinji's earlier train-carriage confrontations from within Unit-01. "Impact" covers Third Impact itself engulfing the world, with only scattered lines left as Asuka's contribution. "Transition" is the re-embodied aftermath: two pilots on a darkling shore, where the strangling and caress finally play out.

Gilham's central hypothesis holds that Asuka is already established as dead before the beach scene — fatally wounded fighting the Mass Production Evangelions, and (it's implied) greeted by Rei much as Ritsuko and Misato were. Her last recorded communication to Shinji during Complementation was "if I have to be with you, I'd rather die" — so on this reading, Shinji's strangling is him giving her exactly what he believes she asked for, not an act of hatred or self-assertion. Her hand on his cheek reads as fond approval that he remembered; his collapse into tears is him "bottling" the act rather than completing it — reinforced by the fact that her caress echoes his mother Yui's own farewell caress just before departing Unit-01 earlier in the film, a memory that would plausibly be what actually breaks his resolve. Under this reading, Asuka's final line isn't disgust at being strangled, but disgusted disappointment that he couldn't go through with it.

Gilham also lays out a considerably darker alternate reading he doesn't rule out — a "Bad End" in which the strangling isn't mercy or self-assertion at all, but simply a continuation of unfinished business from the kitchen-scene confrontation earlier in Complementation: Shinji as "the little squit we already take him for," with Asuka's stillness explained by her being too debilitated to fight back rather than by any acceptance of what's happening. Gilham closes this reading by rendering her final line through a misapplied quotation from Marlowe's Doctor Faustus — Mephistopheles' "Why, this is Hell; nor am I out of it" — casting the ending as a genuine trap rather than any form of catharsis.

entries.title: The backlash that nearly ended Anno's career, and the six months of silence after
entries.body:
After the TV finale aired, Anno faced fierce backlash accusing him of abandoning the plot and being lazy; he read online discussions debating the best way to kill him, stopped wanting to work in animation, and has said he contemplated suicide on two separate occasions. Director and friend Hayao Miyazaki reportedly advised him to take a break before starting work on the film version. Decades later, the 2021 NHK documentary Hideaki Anno: The Final Challenge of Evangelion had Anno describe those threads directly: "People came up with ideas about how to kill me. When I saw that, I lost my will to live. I didn't want to make anime anymore."

Per Studio Khara's own biography of Anno, he withdrew from nearly all creative work for roughly six months immediately after the TV finale aired, producing almost nothing until colleagues talked him into returning to Gainax to adapt the original, unfinished ending into a theatrical film — the project that became Death & Rebirth and then The End of Evangelion.

entries.title: How EvaGate resolved, Anime Expo '96, the home-video rollout, and where the fandom went next
entries.body:
With no public word for two months after the ADV/Gainax rights standoff fans dubbed "EvaGate '96" — during which Gainax was also cracking down on English-language fan sites — GM Yasuhiro Takeda eventually released a statement, via publicity manager Hiroki Sato, that episode 19 would get a partial re-dub, episodes 21-24 would receive "extensive retake footage," and the finale would be remade "using their original scripts." That work became the Director's Cuts (some of it folded into the compilation film Death) and The End of Evangelion. A month later, ADV announced its first VHS volume for August 20, 1996.

At Anime Expo '96 (Anaheim, June 28-30) shortly after, Evangelion won Best New TV Series at the con's awards ceremony and a fan-built Rei figure won the official modeling contest; Anno attended as a guest alongside Noboru Ishiguro, Yoshiaki Kawajiri, Mamoru Oshii, and Kenichi Sonoda — a notably stacked guest lineup even by AX standards. Asked about the finale at his panel there, Anno told the audience, "I have no problem with them. If there's a problem, it's all with you guys. Too bad" — switching to English for the last two words. He said the Eva units were inspired by oni, called Asuka his favorite character ("she's cute"), was surprised American fans preferred Misato over Rei ("They can't handle strong women"), and described Shinji as reflecting his own character "both in conscious and unconscious parts ... I acknowledged that I'm a fool."

ADV's VHS release shipped two episodes per tape from that August through its final volume on July 7, 1998; a parallel laser disc release, starting May 17, 1997, was canceled after two volumes because of disc-rot issues affecting the format. The rec.arts.anime newsgroup that carried most of the era's fan discussion has long since given way to venues like the Evangelion subreddit and EvaGeeks.org, but the pattern it set — Western fans debating a still-airing Japanese show in something close to real time — became the default mode for anime fandom that followed.

entries.title: Seven of the strangest pieces of official Evangelion merchandise
entries.body:
The license has produced some memorably odd tie-ins over the decades. A set of infant onesies paired Evangelion with Rody, the already-unsettling smiling rubber ride-on horse toy previously licensed alongside Hello Kitty and Hatsune Miku, recoloring the built-in horse ears and body to match Units 00, 01, and 02. A tie-in with Kagome's tomato juice restaged an Angel battle with the Eva pilots fighting a giant, ominous tomato in the middle of Tokyo-3, followed by an ad, styled after the show's own Misato-hosted next-episode previews, revealing Shinji and Asuka weren't piloting Evas at all in this version, but giant juice boxes. An ongoing Schick razor campaign, running since 2012, recast a cheerful, clean-shaven Gendo Ikari — a sharp departure from his cold, scheming characterization in the show — as a pitchman for a close shave, alongside a line of Eva-branded razor-holder figures.

Promotion for Tokyo's Shiohaku Expo 2012 included an 18.5-meter (about 61-foot) inflatable Rei Ayanami in her plug suit, seated with one leg replaced by a slide visitors could climb and ride down — reportedly taller than Odaiba's life-size Gundam statue by about two feet. The official Eva Store's line of ordinary household and fashion goods bearing a small Eva-branded charm, patch, or color scheme has included a boxed set of preserved (long-lasting, no-water-needed) flowers that sold for roughly US$126 — an otherwise unremarkable bouquet priced up purely for being dyed in Unit-01's color scheme — and a paired set of "Shinji: Blue Musk" and "kaworu: White Citrus" body sprays, marketed as a "gentle aroma that spreads like the sea and sky" and a "refreshing scent that's clear like water" respectively (a separate three-Eva-Unit body spray line included key art of Rei and Asuka opening Shinji's shirt to spray him). For the franchise's 10th anniversary, figure maker Wave passed over more conventional choices like Misato or Ritsuko and instead redesigned several non-humanoid Angels as "bishōjo" figures: Sachiel came out looking like a busty Rei variant, Tabris (Kaworu's Angel identity) wears a version of Shinji's shirt with Kaworu's hairstyle, and Zeruel was the one design built with LCL-filled breasts, unique in the set.

entries.title: Anno after Evangelion: Love & Pop, marriage, the Rebuild films, and Shin Godzilla
entries.body:
Anno's first professionally released live-action film, Love & Pop (1998), adapts Ryu Murakami's novel about a high schooler drawn into teenage prostitution, shot entirely handheld on consumer digital camcorders — a format he'd later say reawakened the enthusiasm for filmmaking he'd had as a teenager, following straight on from the exhaustion of finishing Evangelion. He also returned to directing anime that year for His and Her Circumstances, adapted concurrently with Masami Tsuda's ongoing manga, but left the production before its final episodes over disagreements with Tsuda about the show's creative direction and merchandising, plus new restrictions TV Tokyo imposed after the unrelated Pokémon seizure incident; Hiroki Satō finished the series in his place, and it would be Anno's last TV anime directing credit for many years.

Anno married Happy Mania creator Moyoco Anno on March 26, 2002; friends and colleagues have said the marriage visibly softened him. (Moyoco's 2005 manga essay Insufficient Direction chronicles the idiosyncrasies of life married to an otaku director, opening with the question "Am I truly prepared to be an otaku's wife?") His Rebuild of Evangelion tetralogy began with Evangelion: 1.0 You Are [Not] Alone (2007) and Evangelion: 2.0 You Can [Not] Advance (2009), both produced with his own Studio Khara alongside Gainax; around 2.0's release, Anno formally resigned from Gainax after roughly 23 years — the two studios parted on reportedly amicable terms at the time, though Anno later sued Gainax in 2016 over unpaid Evangelion royalties and a negligent loan Khara had extended the studio in 2014. Partway through the Rebuild films, he co-directed Shin Godzilla (2016) with Shinji Higuchi, reframing Godzilla's arrival as a modern Japanese bureaucratic crisis explicitly patterned on the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake/tsunami and the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear meltdown; it swept most of the Japan Academy Prizes it was nominated for and became Japan's highest-grossing domestic film that year — Anno's first live-action theatrical release in twelve years.
